#6740. The 18 Best Hotels in Tokyo, From Modern Ryokan to Boutique Hideaways

Millions of visitors flock to Tokyo every year to explore the organized chaos that is one of the world’s most populous cities. Whether it’s the tantalizing food scene, trend-bending fashion, or rich history, the Japanese capital entices every type of traveler. Quite frankly, you could spend months here and barely skim the surface. And choosing your hotel can be just as overwhelming as deciding what to cram into a short visit.

Let’s take it one step at a time and start with where to stay. To help you navigate the thousands of options, we’ve narrowed the list down to some of our favorites; they vary in neighborhood, from frenetic hubs to quieter residential enclaves, so the discerning traveler has a lot to pick from. Some are brand new, others are tried-and-true institutions. Many are from familiar international brands, but a few are the dreamy results of home-grown talent.

One thing to note for winter travelers: Keep in mind that New Year is Japan’s most important holiday. While temples and shrines remain open (and are at their busiest), most businesses and cultural sites are closed for several days—even in a city like Tokyo. If you’ll be in town at the start of the year, it’ll be more important than ever to pick the right hotel to keep you entertained.

With that in mind, here’s our guide to the best hotels in Tokyo.

With just 57 keys—making it the second most intimate property within the Four Seasons portfolio after Naviva in Punta Mita, Mexico—the brand’s exemplary service is brought to the next level here. From Sézanne, the hotel’s lauded French restaurant now under the helm of chef Stephen Lancaster, right down to the reception staff who greet guests by name, you’ll be well looked-after.

In theory, a beautifully textured facade made from salvaged tile fragments should catch the attention of wide-eyed wanderers in a neighborhood that is otherwise modern; after all, we’re talking about Ginza. Here, where the goal is typically to shop until you drop, the last thing you’d expect to come across is a ryokan-inspired hotel hidden away on one of the area’s busiest streets. But that’s exactly what gives Fufu Tokyo Ginza that “if you know, you know” badge of honor.

The hospitality brand is known for its intimate onsen retreats in some of the country’s most popular countryside destinations; this is its first urban outpost. There are just 34 rooms, all of which feature furnished balconies dotted with vegetation and hot spring–fed tubs filled with water ushered in from Atami, the birthplace of Fufu Japan. (Either amenity is hard to come by in this city, but both is simply unheard of.) It only gets better when you head to the lush rooftop terrace, where semi-private banquettes hover above a foot bath. Like with any ryokan, half-board options are available and are worth booking. Dinner features either a sushi omakase or a seasonal kaiseki; and as for the breakfast, it’s easily one of the best in Tokyo.

For its inaugural debut in Japan, 1 Hotel set up shop in Tokyo’s Akasaka district, a central hub for business, entertainment, and dining just a stone’s throw away from other popular enclaves like Azabudai Hills and Roppongi. The brand new property opened this past March, with a whopping 211 accommodations that look out to either Tokyo Tower, the Imperial Palace gardens, or the city skyline. In keeping with the brand’s sustainable sensibilities, single-use plastic is non-existent, filtered water taps are installed in every room, and glassware is made from recycled wine bottles. There’s even a farmstand in the lobby featuring fresh fruit that’s deemed “too imperfect” by farmers to sell at local markets—though it looks fairly flawless by this plebeian’s standards—along with more than 1,500 live plants throughout the entire hotel, including the moss that lines the hallways.

Gin fans will delight in the gorgeous lobby bar, where you can choose from nearly 100 locally crafted varieties under a ceiling that’s inspired by karesansui (Zen gardens). At NiNi restaurant, vegetables are the star of the breakfast spread; the rest of the day calls for French Riviera cuisine with a Japanese twist, like a kabocha pumpkin soup de pistou. And if you have time for a dip, you’ll find an indoor pool with a beautiful outdoor terrace just next to the spa.

Every few years there’s a hotel that garners so much attention it becomes an icon before it even opens. In 2024, that title belonged to Janu Tokyo. The flagship of Aman’s long-awaited sister brand, Janu Tokyo trades in zen and serenity for a more energetic approach to hospitality, perhaps best exhibited by the property’s whopping eight food and beverage venues. The hotel also offers a robust wellness center that spans four floors, housing one of the city’s largest gyms, a 25-meter pool, and an extensive spa. Once you’re ready to retire, spacious rooms with largely monochromatic interiors welcome you with soaking tubs and balconies in most instances.

Bookended by action with the heart of Shibuya on one side and Harajuku at the other, there’s a lot happening around Trunk(Hotel) Cat Street. In addition to its stellar location, this lifestyle boutique property has managed to capture the zeitgeist, turning it into a favored haunt for the neighborhood’s effortlessly cool inhabitants. The lobby lounge, with a café by day and bar by night, doubles as a co-working space and is quite the scene at nearly all hours. Upstairs are just 15 accommodations ranging from cozy rooms to residential-style suites, all accented with custom Japan-made adornments utilizing upcycled materials.

The hotel offers two on-site restaurants—one that serves Japanese-inflected international fare, the other a yakitori (skewered meats and vegetables) spot—and its own version of a convenience store with locally sourced bites and a curated selection of sustainable products.

Remote destinations have been a part of Aman’s ethos since its inception—the opening of the Tokyo property in 2014 marked the brand’s first true city project. Resident architect Kerry Hill’s minimalist approach to the group’s luxury-defining properties arguably plays the most natural role in Japan, a country where less is more. The vaulted atrium in the lobby, which is a hot spot for afternoon tea, has become an icon of sorts within Aman’s portfolio, as has the stone-clad, 30-meter pool overlooking the city. Its bright and airy rooms are some of the largest in the city (the smallest coming in at 71 square meters), and are characterized by light wood and low-profile furnishings. Slide the shoji screen back to reveal a stone bathroom, complete with a window-side ofuro tub with uninterrupted views.

Hotel Groove Shinjuku offers a more approachable price point than its sister property Bellustar Tokyo while still benefiting from the same shiny new tower and prime location. Entry-level rooms are cozy, but there are plenty of larger options (at relatively reasonable rates) like the Japanese Suite, which features a tatami-mat floor spacious enough for multiple futons, making it highly popular with families. Colorful carpets accent the otherwise neutral-hued accommodations while the artist-designed suites up the ante on personality. And if you’re here for a lengthier stay, the on-site coin-operated laundry is an unexpectedly wonderful touch.

Top-floor occupancy of a high-rise is commonplace for luxury hotels in Tokyo; it’s no different at the Four Seasons’ second outpost in the city. When you exit the elevators on the 39th floor, you’re greeted by a tranquil water feature that draws inspiration from the Imperial Palace’s moat. In fact, the royal residence (and the sprawling metropolis’ skyline) can be seen from various points throughout the hotel, including the lobby lounge, where afternoon tea is served, and many of its 190 rooms. Speaking of accommodations, they’re spacious here, as to be expected from a Four Seasons, with floor-to-ceiling windows offering plenty of natural lighting and panoramic views. And if you’re looking to set your eyes on Tokyo Skytree, head down to the heated indoor pool for a couple of laps, then cool off in one of the mist chairs.

When hunger strikes there are a few on-site dining options to choose from, including the all-day Italian restaurant Pigneto (the hand-tossed Neapolitan pizzas are the highlight); but the crown jewels are Est and Virtù, both of which are worth visiting even if you’re not a staying guest. At the former you’ll find refined take on contemporary French cuisine with a commitment to sourcing nearly all ingredients from around Japan and a seasonal menu. Meanwhile, the French-Japanese love affair continues at the latter in the form of cocktails, where spirits from both destinations are the star. The Smoked Ume Fashioned is a prefect representation of the concept, which uses a homemade brandy umeshu with plums that have been aged for at least six months, as is the Yuzu Nagi, where yuzu gin meets cognac in a bright, citrus-forward tipple. (Make sure to ask for the seasonal cocktail menu, where you might just find a kakigori-inspired drink, and order the lobster okonomiyaki, an elevated take on the Japanese classic.)

Back in 1962 when Japan was in the midst of an economic boom, the Okura was one of Tokyo’s preeminent hotels, playing host to a number of dignitaries during its tenure. So when it announced its closure in 2015 with a full demolition in tow—on par with the Japanese affinity for rebuilding rather than renovating, as exhibited with the country’s holiest shrine, Ise Jingu—the decision caused quite the stir amongst locals. Nevertheless, the Okura was reborn in 2019 with two glitzy new towers. Some of its history was preserved, like the original mid-century modern chairs that have since been reupholstered, the signature pentagon-faceted lanterns, and kumiko lattice woodwork seen throughout the property.

The main building, dubbed Prestige, is largely geared toward business travelers. The other (the Heritage Wing) appeals more to leisure travelers. All accommodations are suites with sumptuous, oversized bathrooms, complete with a jet tub and private sauna. Some even boast balconies—a rarity in the city. While you’re here make sure to check out Yamazato, a high-end Japanese restaurant with dedicated sushi and tempura counters, along with a visit to the spa for what is arguably one of the better massages in the city.

In a city ruled by skyscrapers, finding some greenery in the middle of Tokyo is like a glass of ice water on a hot summer day. That’s what you get at Takanawa Hanakohro. Part of the larger Prince Hotels compound near Shinagawa Station, the ambiance is set by a classic garden complete with a koi pond, over 200 sakura trees, and the hotel’s very own temple. And while Takanawa Hanakohro occupies one of the complex’s three towers, what makes it particularly special is its 16 ryokan-style suites. Characterized by tatami floors, shoji screens, and large bathrooms with a tub, they’re about as traditional as you get, with courteous service by kimono-clad staff to match. A stay here comes with unfettered access to all of the four executive lounges, including Oh-Sai, which is reserved only for Hanakohro guests, along with a dedicated spa. And while breakfast is usually served at Oh-Sai, you can also request an in-room delivery; the best option, if you’re staying in one of the garden view rooms.

The business district of Otemachi is perhaps one of the most unsuspecting locations for a ryokan, but that’s what makes a tranquil retreat like Hoshinoya Tokyo even more special. Upon entering, the cacophony of the bustling metropolis instantly dissipates and is replaced by a relaxing aura. You’re greeted by a diligent attendant who stores your shoes in one of the bamboo and chestnut cubbies lining the walls, welcoming you to walk barefoot on the tatami mat floors.

With the exception of the restaurants (which includes a recently added sushi bar), the hotel is strictly reserved for guests. And while there are 84 rooms in total, each floor only has six accommodations, creating a sense of intimacy as though every level is its own mini ryokan, along with a shared ochanoma lounge that’s stocked with complimentary snacks like onigiri and an array of seasonal teas. Enjoy spacious digs with low furnishings, deep soaking tubs, and traditional Japanese design elements like shoji screens, but while you’re here make sure to head up to the rooftop onsen and soak in the healing properties of the natural hot spring.

Hoshino Resorts has several brands under its umbrella—including the uber-luxe Hoshinoya—but at the opposite end of the spectrum is OMO, a more budget-conscious collection of hotels that feature compact but well-appointed rooms. At OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda the accommodations start at 200 square feet; ideal for solo travelers who want something more comfortable than a hostel without breaking the bank. Suites are just a little over 600 square feet. Most have sofas by the window so that you can enjoy the city views in comfort, and there is also a bunk-style room that’s great for families or a small group of friends.

But the real highlight here is being immersed in the lesser-explored Gotanda district, where you’ll find culinary gems like tonkatsu institution Tonki, famed reservation-only izakaya Shokudo Todaka, and stand-up udon bar Oniyanma (this particular store is arguably better than its other locations in the city).

Ginza has no shortage of luxury hotels to complement its high-end stores. Just north of the city’s most glamorous shopping district is relative newcomer Bulgari Hotel Tokyo, which opened in 2023. Set directly across from Tokyo Station, the glitzy 98-key property blends its roots with its new environs through contemporary Italian design and time-honored Japanese craftsmanship. Bulgari fans will also appreciate overt nods to the brand in the form of framed sketches from the archives, the jeweler’s 1970s Mount Fuji brooch on display in the gallery, and the house’s signature eight-point star inlaid in the black granite floor of the reception area.

The mark of any stellar city hotel is when it’s enticing enough to keep you indoors despite an exciting metropolis waiting to be explored, and Bulgari Hotel Tokyo delivers. To start, the accommodations are incredibly spacious, starting from 51 square meters. And while there are plenty of luxe touches—throws crafted in Kyoto, hand-brushed gold ceilings, Bulgari-branded bathroom amenities—the automatic blinds are the winner, opening every time you step into the room to reveal panoramic vistas of the city and, in some cases, Mount Fuji on a clear day. Looking for even more dramatic views? Head up to the 45th-floor rooftop lounge, where you’ll be met with Venetian terrazzo flooring and a beautiful glass mosaic wall of birds and trees behind the sleek bar, flanked by lush terraces with plenty of seating looking out to a seemingly endless skyline.

But whatever you do, don’t forget to carve out some time for the spa. There, you’ll find a 25-meter pool clad in reflective green and gold tiles, surrounded by daybeds and floor-to-ceiling windows.

Just blocks from Harajuku and Omotesando Hills, the Aoyama Grand Hotel is arguably one of the most underrated gems in Tokyo. Joining the latest crop of stylish boutique hotels to pop up in the city, the property features plush rooms with mid-century modern decor and punchy patterns that add a quirky character. It offers guests a host of amenities that aren’t even found at hotels commanding double its price tag, such as a complimentary minibar inclusive of alcoholic beverages and snacks as well as bicycles to explore the surrounding area. And while there are a handful of on-site dining concepts, the two standouts are Shikaku, a countertop restaurant serving comforting Japanese fare, and the Top, an alfresco rooftop lounge with a DJ every weekend.

While Shibuya is known for its frenetic energy, things slow down a bit just north of the station in Tomigaya. The trendy neighborhood has been popular for quite some time amongst well-heeled locals, but it’s now drawing in discerning jet-setters thanks to Trunk(Hotel) Yoyogi Park. In stark contrast to its lively and cool sister hotel on the other side of Shibuya, this new property is serene and understated, providing an urban sanctuary just a stone’s throw away from one of Tokyo’s most exciting enclaves. Japandi interiors are the shared work of Keiji Ashizawa Design and Copenhagen-based Norm Architects, setting the stage for a relaxing stay. Its crown jewel, though? The pool club. Open only to guests, the heated infinity oasis looks out at the lush treetops of Yoyogi Park and is complemented by a jacuzzi, sunken fire pit, and oyster bar.

Crowning the new 47-floor Tokyu Kabukicho Tower—where you’ll also find a cinema, nightclub, arcade, and yokocho-style food hall amongst other facilities—Bellustar Tokyo is the perfect hideaway for those who want to be in the thick of Shinjuku without feeling like they are. It’s just steps from the buzzy district’s famed attractions like Golden Gai, a grid of narrow alleys filled to the brim with tiny bars and restaurants, but once you’re whisked up to the sleek lobby, chaos softens into tranquility.

Spacious, minimalist rooms are outfitted with deep tubs and floor-to-ceiling windows to capitalize on their sky-high position (the view alone is worth spending the night in). When it comes to the penthouses, enjoy the benefits of a butler service, a fully equipped kitchen, and access to a dedicated lounge stocked with champagne and small bites. Sora, the largest, also boasts an en-suite spa.

Topping Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower, the Mandarin Oriental is the neighborhood’s premier address. The luxurious group’s signature aesthetic of rich hues and supple fabrics carries over to its Tokyo property with the addition of Japanese design elements like paper lamps and traditional kimono patterns. Spacious accommodations are outfitted with luxurious bathrooms, oversized windows, plush beds, and a bonsai tree for a welcomed touch of greenery. Service, like at any MO, is attentive, and the four-handed massage might be the best way to beat jet lag. While you’re here, explore the immediate area. At the hotel’s doorstep, you’ll find centuries-old businesses still in operation today, a brilliant launching point for discovering Japanese traditions and souvenir shopping.

The Peninsula Hotels has accrued quite a loyal fanbase for its top-notch service, luxurious accommodations with spa-like bathrooms, and its incredible fleet of Rolls-Royces. You can expect all of this at its Tokyo outpost, where doormen donned in the group’s signature white uniform greet you with doors wide open. Rooms nod to Japanese craftsmanship with ajiro ceilings and tochinoki wood doors, and are extremely spacious, with walk-in closets and bathtubs. Beat jet lag with a few laps at the 20-meter pool or make use of your in-room yoga mat and foam roller. Then, head down to the lobby for an unforgettable breakfast. In addition to Japanese and Chinese sets, there’s also a plant-based option inspired by shojin ryori, a Japanese Buddhist cuisine. All three are phenomenal and some of the best in the city.

#6737. These MacBook Deals Are Good Enough to Shop Before Black Friday

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Considering the price of tech, we’ll gladly take $250 off a new MacBook.

If there’s one Apple product line where the recent price hikes hit the hardest, it’s the MacBook. Rising RAM and storage costs have pushed laptop prices up across the board, which makes scoring a new MacBook on sale all the more mission critical.

As luck would have it, Black Friday deals on Apple tech are already ramping up on Amazon, including discounts on MacBooks. While there’s always the chance these deals might continue to deepen in the next week, the current discounts are nothing to sneeze at if you can’t wait that long to shop.

Of course, not all MacBooks were created equal. While the standard MacBook Air is great for most, those who are planning on running hardcore software might be benefit from a beefed-up MacBook Pro. And if budget is your primary concern, we’re of the opinion that the MacBook Neo is a worthy buy, even if it’s only $50 off right now.

The best MacBook Air deal you’ll find right now is this $250 discount on the 15-inch model. With this laptop, you’ll get Apple’s M5 chip in a fanless, 3.3-pound frame that handles heavy multitasking and light video editing without breaking a sweat. Base storage doubled to 512 GB this year—a great upgrade for storing more apps, photos, and files—and the 15.3-inch Liquid Retina display is sharp and vivid. You also get a 12 MP Center Stage camera that’s great on video calls, WiFi 7 for fast downloads, and up to 18 hours of battery, enough for a busy workday and then some. It won’t replace a MacBook Pro for serious creative work or gaming, but for school, business, and general use, it’s the one to get.

Deals on 13-inch models aren’t as steep—yet. But we expect that to change in a week’s time.

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 15-inch (M5, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB)

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 13-inch (M5, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB)

Apple 2026 MacBook Air 13-Inch (M5, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB)

Given that Apple just dropped a new slate of M6 MacBook Pros, in addition to the company’s first-ever touchscreen laptop, we were anticipating discounts on the M5 range to clear out inventory. In the lead-up to Black Friday, you can shave $200 off of the 14-inch model, complete with a Liquid Retina XDR display with 120Hz ProMotion, up to 24 hours of battery, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, an SD card slot, and up to 2 TB of storage.

Why go Pro over the Air? The GPU is fast, which makes a difference when editing video, working with high-res photos, or gaming, and the XDR screen is significantly brighter. If your daily workload has started becoming too much for the Air to handle, this is where you should look next. If you want the biggest, most powerful model possible, souped-up MacBook Pros are up to $500 off.

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 16-Inch (M5 Max, 36 GB RAM, 2 TB)

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 14-Inch (M5 Pro, 24 GB RAM, 1 TB)

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 16-Inch (M5 Pro, 24 GB RAM, 2 TB)

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop, even with the recent price hike from $599 to $699. Right now, the Neo is modestly discounted, although we’re holding out hope that it might drop down to its inaugural price—or even lower—once Black Friday proper arrives. The Neo is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for their first Mac. It runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip and is surprisingly quick for browsing, sending email, and streaming video. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display looks great for the price, and the battery lasts a solid 16 hours. It also comes in four fun colors, with the yellow-green citrus being a fan favorite.

There are some trade-offs with going with Apple’s budget model, including storage that starts at 256 GB, just 8 GB of RAM, and no keyboard backlight. You also get only two USB-C ports, so getting a USB-C hub is a must if you plan to connect a lot of accessories. Spending an extra $100 gets you a Neo with 512 GB of storage and a Touch ID sensor for quick unlocking. For students or anyone who mostly sends emails and browses the Web, the Neo is hard to beat.

#6736. 10 Airbnbs in New Mexico to Book This Winter, from Santa Fe and Beyond

There’s something undeniably magical about New Mexico, especially in the colder months. Chile ristras line front porches, ski season revs up in Taos, and farolitos light the streets in December. The days are sunny and dry, but nights are cold enough for a kiva fireplace or a hot tub soak under the stars. It makes for a different kind of trip than a cozy New England getaway or fall foliage-inspired cabin retreat, the desert awash in sunset hues. Plus, New Mexico is prime road-trip territory, with its wide-open highways and dramatic landscape shifts.

From the powdery white dunes of White Sands National Park to the art-saturated streets of Santa Fe, the state has inspired artists and creative types for years upon years. Whether you want to lose yourself in the vast vistas that captivated Georgia O'Keeffe or spend a long weekend gallery-hopping and market-browsing in Santa Fe, we've rounded up a selection of Airbnbs that feel as distinctive as the state itself to serve as your home base.

Ahead, 10 New Mexico rentals that sit at the intersection of design and desert living.

Artfully designed by fashion designer Raquel Allegra, the 8,000-square-foot space sits on five acres in a quiet canyon about 20 minutes from Taos Ski Valley. The interiors are anchored by signature New Mexican architectural features such as arched windows, white plaster walls, high ceilings, and wood-burning kiva fireplaces, while the furnishings are design-forward yet restrained, allowing the home’s bones to really sing.

With six bedrooms, it’s an expansive enough space for a ski trip with friends or a creative group retreat; one Vogue writer even booked it for an off-the-beaten-path bachelorette. Radiant heated floors and a steady supply of firewood keep the home toasty after a day on the slopes. And with no cell service available near the home, it’s very much your chance to completely unplug.

Amenities: Radiant heating, wood-burning kiva fireplaces, furnished porch, WiFi, garden views

Location: Taos Ski Valley, Taos, New Mexico

This 1940s Santa Fe adobe, once a corner store, is now an art gallery-like home whose walls are dotted with more than 50 nichos (small, recessed niches carved into the plaster). They’re a staple of Southwestern and Spanish colonial architecture, each lit like a museum case and, in the case of this property, filled with ceramics and other artful pieces.

Polished white cement floors and a white oak kitchen give the entire home the feeling of a clean palette; a calming backdrop for whatever your Santa Fe vacation holds. Its four bedrooms make it a good fit for a family ski trip, with Ski Santa Fe 30 minutes away and a hot tub and fire pit waiting in the private backyard for your return. The River Trail is a block away, Canyon Road is close by, and dogs are welcome.

Amenities: Kiva fireplace, hot tub, firepit, soaking tub, chef’s kitchen, gated parking, dog-friendly

This hacienda was once a neighborhood shop where horses and burros carrying firewood were hitched out front. Today, sunny windows open onto a bright living room, and the house has three kiva fireplaces, shelves packed tightly with books and board games, and a renovated kitchen you can make your own during your stay.

Between the three bedrooms and the den (which has a sofa bed), this home sleeps eight, and two adjacent units can be rented for larger groups. Galleries and restaurants are right on its doorstep, too.

Amenities: Three kiva fireplaces, Sonos sound system, renovated kitchen, two private patios, washer and dryer

This listing has been high up on our Airbnb wishlist for years. Located in Abiquiu, not too far from O’Keeffe’s famed Ghost Ranch, this adobe sits squarely in the middle of 10 shared acres in the high desert landscape that drew O'Keeffe (and generations of artists and photographers after her) in.

This recently renovated home is a quiet base for exploring one of New Mexico's most creatively charged regions. The traditional architecture is intact with thick walls, desert light, wood beams, stone fireplaces, and classic New Mexican tile floors. The interiors are peppered with both man-made and natural relics, like a Noguchi-style hanging paper lantern or a sculptural tumbleweed hanging from the ceiling. It’s the kind of place O'Keeffe herself might have booked.

Amenities: Full kitchen, washer/dryer, mini-split AC and heating throughout, mountain views, dedicated workspace, WiFi

Designed by architect Bart Prince and featured in Architectural Digest, this sculptural home at the base of the Sandia Mountains is definitely a one-of-a-kind experience. Six viewing decks offer panoramic views of the mountains above and Albuquerque's city lights below, while floor-to-ceiling windows blur the line between indoors and out. A private hiking trail on the property connects directly to Sandia Peak; meaning the National Forest is essentially your backyard.

Amenities: 6 viewing decks, private hiking trail, floor-to-ceiling windows

Location: Sandia Mountains, Albuquerque, New Mexico

This mid-century adobe sits in Casa Alegre, a leafy pocket of Santa Fe’s Midtown District, where you’re a block from the River Trail and close to the galleries and shows at the El Rey. A traditional kiva fireplace anchors the living room, Sonos speakers run throughout, and one of the bedrooms comes with a cozy reading nook. With three bedrooms and a fully fenced yard, it works well for families young kids who want their own space for their holiday in the desert. On winter nights, the hot tub will be an especially beloved feature.

Amenities: Kiva fireplace, hot tub, Sonos sound system, fenced yard, washer and dryer, parking for three cars, dog friendly

Casa de la Cruz is a traditional adobe, built with stucco, giant vigas, and thick walls that stay warm in winter and cool in summer. The interiors reflect the Southwest aesthetic with wrought-iron light fixtures paired with Navajo blankets and pillows, leather sofas, and rustic, worn furniture sprinkled throughout.

Set on 12 acres abutting Carson National Forest in Abiquiu, the property has three kiva fireplaces, radiant heated floors, and a private box canyon to explore—which is an incredible selling point on its own. Plus, you can’t beat the location with Ghost Ranch being just 30 minutes away, the hot springs of Ojo Caliente another 30, and downtown Santa Fe under an hour, as well.

Amenities: Private box canyon, outdoor fire pit, full kitchen, outdoor grill, Starlink WiFi, 3 fireplaces, radiant heated floors

This charming home is located in Dixon—a small artist's village in the hills of Northern New Mexico—with wilderness walks straight from the door. The bones are traditional New Mexico adobe architecture with viga ceilings, Southwestern decor, works from local artists, and a newly remodeled kitchen. Surrounded by pinyon and sage bush views alongside the mountains, its exceptionally quiet and gorgeous sunsets are best taken in from the plush ramada with its built-in banco seating.

Amenities: Ramada, full kitchen, streaming TV, AppleTV, WiFi, central heating, pet-friendly

Featured in Dwell, this off-grid Earthship (a fitting description) outside Taos is a rare rental that beautifully intersects luxury and sustainability. The structure collects rainwater, generates its own solar power, grows food indoors, and uses water three times over—all without sacrificing comfort. Adobe interiors, a south-facing greenhouse, and whimsical touches (like a stained-glass mermaid) keep things interesting in the best way.

Amenities: Off-grid solar power, rainwater collection, indoor greenhouse, turntable, bluetooth, WiFi

This newly built guesthouse is part of the H.H. Dorman estate, rumored to have hosted D.H. Lawrence, Georgia O'Keeffe, Ansel Adams, and Aldous Huxley in the 1920s. The two-bedroom, two-bath home, which shares the grounds with the historic main house, is a short walk to Santa Fe plaza and features vaulted ceilings, a gas fireplace, one-of-a-kind antiques, and art throughout. It boasts two private courtyards, one with an outdoor dining area and another with a fire pit and hot tub, which guests are welcome to enjoy.

Amenities: Private hot tub, fire pit, two courtyards, full kitchen, gas fireplace, washer/dryer, gated parking

#6735. The AI Police Are Going After Black Writers

The white powers that be have always doubted our intellect. Now they have a new tool.

Picture a waifish enslaved teen—a girl named Phillis, after the slave ship that Middle Passaged her from present-day Senegal and Gambia—trembling before a room of incredulous, austere white men, the most esteemed thinkers and politicians of colonial Massachusetts. The reason: The gifted girl wrote a book manuscript, and the family that owned her journeyed all the way to London to find a publisher for it. That prospective British publisher, a bloke named Archibald Bell, promised to publish the manuscript if the Wheatleys could prove Phillis had written it herself—an attestation tantamount, of course, to whether an enslaved African soon-to-be American possessed the intellect requisite to producing exceptional creative work.

Present at the trial, which has been described by historian Henry Louis Gates Jr. as the nascent scene of African American letters, was Thomas Hutchinson, the governor of the Province of the Massachusetts Bay; Andrew Oliver, the province’s lieutenant governor; and Mr. John Hancock himself, the future first governor of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Per Gates, almost all the men forgathered to pass judgment on Phillis Wheatley were both Harvard graduates and slaveholders. No record exists of what transpired, but oh how brilliant Phillis must’ve been as she convinced those 18 eminent Bostonians that she’d indeed written the poems. The confirmation was printed in the front matter of Phillis’s poetry collection—the first book published by an African soon-to-be American—Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773):

We whose Names are under-written, do assure the World, that the Poems specified in the following Page, were . . . written by Phillis, a young Negro Girl, who was but a few Years since, brought an uncultivated Barbarian from Africa, and has ever since been, and now is, under the Disadvantage of serving as a Slave in a Family in this Town. She has been examined by some of the best Judges, and is thought qualified to write them.

As my great-grandmother Edith Larkin Jackson, a woman not two generations removed from chattel slavery, used to say, “There’s nothing new under the sun.” Mama Eddie was a schoolteacher, and I imagine she’d be astounded by artificial intelligence. However, she’d have no trouble whatsoever fathoming a world that called into question the creativity or intellect of her people.

Here we are in this brave new world of AI, an age hurtling headlong toward the peril of superintelligence. Here we are in the 21st century, a time when the ivory-tower panjandrums are engaged in a sinister pattern, if not conspiratorial scheme, of incriminating Black and brown writers with even the suggestion that their work is AI assisted.

For example: In March, Hachette Book Group rendered kaput the U. S. publication of Mia Ballard’s Shy Girl over claims of AI usage.

When Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir’s story “The Serpent in the Grove” was named the regional winner of the Commonwealth Prize in May, Ethan Mollick, a Wharton Business School professor who serves as the codirector of Wharton Generative AI Labs, ran it through the AI-detection software Pangram, touted as the industry standard, and reported that the platform flagged it at 100 percent. Once Mollick shared his findings on social media, several others joined the chorus bemoaning Nazir’s work as a product of AI.

In July, academics studying AI accused H. M. Wolfe of having used a large language model to write her best seller Daggermouth (though its publisher Simon & Schuster has, thus far, stood by the book). Later that month, writer Jerry Falade had a $2 million book deal with Macmillan collapse after his agents withdrew the submission of his debut crime novel citing AI concerns.

In September, Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça ou Mourir (It Was Either That or Die) was proclaimed a standout of the French literary season, won France’s Prix du Roman FNAC, and was long-listed for the Goncourt, the country’s most prestigious literary prize. But then an anonymous X account (later revealed to be owned by a conservative columnist) posted that Pangram had identified all 34 chapters of the book as having been written with AI. That claim spurred accusations that Orélien plagiarized earlier work, leading the Goncourt to nix the book from its long list.

In October, The Atlantic accused writer Simbarashe Kundizeza of using AI to write “The Blue Fighter,” which won the Caine Prize, Africa’s most prestigious short-story accolade.

Germane: While Nazir is Trinidadian, Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Orélien, and Kundizeza are all Black.

Although all those writers have denied claims of using AI to produce their work, I’m not here to dispute whether they did or to what degree they used it, nor the epistemological paradox of using AI to determine whether a writer used AI to write a story. Of equal importance is that, if we ain’t reached the point where all published writing is scanned for possible use of an LLM, what’s the logic informing which writers are investigated for AI use and which aren’t, as well as the attendant issue of which accused writers suffer the most severe fallout, including the scarlet letter of damaged credibility?

The plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be judged in light of what’s being described as an era of postliteracy. Of the specter of AI sloptimism becoming so ubiquitous it overruns human output. Of the cataclysmic doom of superintelligence approximating the creative work of a human brain to such a degree that the difference will be negligible to the undiscerning masses.

The plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be apprehended against the beef between the publishing industry writ large and AI. Against 10,000 authors having copublished an “empty” book in protest of their work being pirated to train its models. Against America’s Big Five publishers suing Meta for copyright infringement. Against the recent unsealed documents that reveal OpenAI executives knew they were training their AI on copyrighted material and, furthermore, that AI-authored books were apt to displace in the market ones authored by humans. “There will be a point where a bunch of artists express worry about what we’re doing here, and we’ll likely ignore their concerns and release anyway,” OpenAI policy director Jack Clark wrote in an internal memo back in 2020. The predicament of Black and brown writers should be weighed against the long and calculated history of portraying them as lesser intellects.

Casting doubt on the possibility of Black literary brilliance is in the spirit of a hubristic Saul Bellow asking, “Who is the Tolstoy of the Zulus?” Of 45/47 portraying beaucoup Black people as “not that bright.” Of attacking DEI to paint us as unworthy or incapable, less we are sanctioned by people in power. The same insidious forces—linked to right-wing Cambridge professor James Orr and conservative billionaire Peter Thiel—stoked the allegations that ended in Cambridge professor Jason Arday dying by suicide. (Arday has been posthumously cleared of plagiarism.)

In stark contrast, best-selling novelist and screenwriter Anthony Horowitz has admitted using AI for his work. Best-selling biographer Katie Prescott extolled AI as invaluable in writing her book on Mike Lynch, the late British tech entrepreneur and AI pioneer. And while she’s been called among other things a “grifter” and a “villain,” South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books using artificial intelligence since 2025 and defended her use of LLMs despite criticism and threats. While she later clarified she used it only for research, Nobel laureate Olga Tokarczuk caused a ruckus revealing she queried AI for writing help. Other than Santiago Schnell, a white Latino, resigning as the provost of Dartmouth for using AI in his published articles and The New York Times cutting ties with Alex Preston for an AI-assisted book review, beyond vocal to tepid criticism, white writers aren’t suffering material consequences on par with those of their Black peers.

Poor Phillis Wheatley never published a second book. Despite advertising six times in the newspaper to find a publisher. Despite announcing she’d dedicate it to Benjamin Franklin. Despite General George Washington extolling her as “favored by the muses.” In fact, in 1784, Phillis died at 30 years young, destitute, having placed the last advertisement for her second manuscript just a few months prior.

Because Big Tech is big-time thriving and race is evermore an oppressive tool, critics are bound to keep casting the work of Black writers as AI assisted, in effect electing themselves nouveau versions of those privileged 18th-century Bostonians. Best believe their indictments are a tacit way to portray the work of Black people as unworthy of patronage, acclaim, awards—aka inferior. But be forewarned: If Big Tech succeeds at AI turning the creative work of human brains passé if not obsolete, it’s near foregone that most writers will lose their ability to earn a living. Indeed, the sad-ass upshot is that if AI prevails, all writers—race be damned—will be fated a Phillis.

#6732. Where to Stay in Jamaica for a Tropical Winter Sun Getaway

If you’re anything like me, entering the land of 4:50 p.m. sunsets means it’s time to a) cry a little and b) book a tropical vacation as soon as possible. In my experience, Jamaica has always been the perfect antidote to cold-weather blues; I’ve been nearly every winter for the past decade. This season, the island is still rebuilding after Hurricane Melissa made landfall last October, but its recovery—and tourism comeback—has been inspiring. Jamaica truly has it all, from iconic music and fashion to pristine beaches, lush rainforests, fresh (and absolutely delicious) food, and a long tradition of Hollywood and royal cachet.

As for where to stay? The boutique hotel scene is unmatched. While Jamaica does have its fair share of big-box, could-be-anywhere all-inclusives, the top hotels are the complete opposite and ooze charm.

Whether you want to drink rum punches on the cliffs of Negril, go hiking in the lush jungles of Port Antonio, or simply hang on the beach as the soft sounds of reggae drift through the air, these 12 options make it easy to experience the country’s vibrant creative culture for yourself. Just be prepared to get hooked, if you aren’t already.

Unless you live your life like a disgruntled White Lotus guest, it’s basically impossible to be in a bad mood at Rockhouse. Located on the western tip of Negril, the 40-room hotel—which celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2024—has all the ingredients for a good time. It’s built into Negril’s limestone cliffs, for starters, so the cliff jumping is next-level. The stone and thatched-roof villas are thoroughly charming; many of them have bright red ladders that allow you to climb directly down into the turquoise sea (which you should, especially first thing in the morning after a steaming mug of Blue Mountain coffee…heaven). The food is great, too, with fresh local dishes like callaloo omelets and moringa smoothies made with ingredients from the property’s on-site organic garden.

But really, you book this spot for the energy. Artists, designers, and other creatives frequent the property for its lively atmosphere and stylish crowd. I’ve personally stayed at Rockhouse twice myself—first with my mom and sister for a mother-daughter trip, and then with my two best friends for our 40th birthdays last year—and it was all smiles both times. My girlfriends and I still reminisce about our endless rum punches at the infinity pool bar, where the bartenders were so much fun, we momentarily forgot our bodies cannot handle mainlining cocktails like we once could. Luckily, that’s what hangover swims are for.

Amenities: three on-site restaurants, spa, infinity pool, weekly psilocybin sound bath experience, complimentary shuttles to Skylark Negril, daily morning yoga, candle-making workshops, and Rockhouse Foundation community tours

Bonus tip: The traditional bathing soak at the spa is heavenly: Tubs are filled with flower petals, herbs, botanicals, and your choice of aromatherapy oil.

Address: West End Road, Negril, Westmoreland

While the cliffs at Rockhouse are undoubtedly delightful, sometimes you just want to spend the day on the sand. And for that, Skylark—which opened as Rockhouse’s sister property in 2018—is the perfect choice. The 43-room boutique hotel holds a prime location right on Seven Mile Beach; not just a beach, but the beach in Negril. Skylark’s spot in the sand stands out for its yellow-and-white striped umbrellas and aqua loungers that match the sea.

Venture past the beach and you’ll notice the hotel’s mod, tropical design. While Rockhouse leans more rustic, Skylark is a bit of a throwback, with a very retro Miami Beach feel (think: black-and-white checkered floors and pops of pastel pink). And then there’s the Miss Lily’s of it all. Back in 2011, the team behind Rockhouse opened the Jamaican restaurant in Soho to bring the spirit of Rockhouse back home to New York, where it quickly acquired a cult following. So when Skylark announced it would open the first Miss Lily’s outpost in Jamaica itself, the superfans went wild—myself included. I’ve been twice now, and must say it feels extra special to enjoy their signature jerk chicken with a side of tropical breeze. Once the sun goes down, DJs take over with nightly sets of the country’s latest reggae and dancehall.

Amenities: rooftop spa, complimentary beach loungers, tents, and umbrellas, boutique and gift shop, beachside service from Miss Lily’s, daily shuttle to sister hotel Rockhouse

Bonus tip: Don’t miss the boutique’s Sweet Like JAM section, featuring high-end designers from across the African and Caribbean diaspora (like Diotima, Tribe Nine Studios, Theophilio, and Bianca Saunders), all curated by stylist and fashion editor Mecca James-Williams.

Address: Norman Manley Boulevard, Negril, Westmoreland

The secret’s certainly out about Geejam. This secluded hilltop hideaway is located in Port Antonio, a port town on Jamaica’s lush, lesser-visited northeastern coast. Built by two former music executives as a residential recording studio in 1998, the property eventually expanded into a boutique hotel in 2008 and has hosted everyone from Bad Bunny to Rihanna to Amy Winehouse (to Drake, Megan Thee Stallion, Harry Styles, Florence and the Machine, The Rolling Stones…the list goes on).

But despite its celeb appeal, Geejam somehow retains has the feel of an undiscovered gem. There are four wooden jungle cabins (named Ska, Rocksteady, Mento, and Drum & Bass, after Jamaica’s popular music genres), 12 guestrooms, a three-bedroom villa, and two premium villas with a dedicated staff. Many are built into the property’s six acres of rainforest so discreetly, you could miss them if you’re not looking. The main open-air bar and lounge, Bushbar, is just as low-profile: When my husband and I dropped in for a cocktail on a recent visit to “Portie,” (as the locals call it) we wondered if we were in the right place. A few guests were playing pool on the vintage billiard table, others were milling about the actual pool deck, and mellow reggae was playing softly in the background. Surely, we thought, a hotel this legendary would feel a bit more…scene-y? But of course, that understated vibe is precisely the point. It extends to the property’s new restaurant and bar, Bentley’s, which opened on their private, tucked-away beach in 2025 and serves a mix of Jamaican specialties and homemade pizza.

Amenities: recording studio, private beach with kayaking and paddleboarding, outdoor infinity pool, two main restaurants/bars, spa services, gym with private trainers available to book, pool table, treehouse DJ booth, various wedding and event spaces

Bonus tip: Portland is known for its waterfalls, rainforest hikes, river rafting, and iconic spring-fed Blue Lagoon—so tempting as it may be to hole up in your cabin, be sure to explore a little, too (the hotel’s custom excursions team can help with that). Don’t miss fresh lobster from Cynthia’s on Winnifred Beach; just call her a day ahead to place your order.

Address: 122 Skippers Boulevard, Port Antonio, Portland

Most people who visit Jamaica tend to stick to the main coastal towns of Negril, Montego Bay, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio. But the country’s lush Blue Mountains—home to the legendary, eponymous coffee—are worth adding to your itinerary, too. And there is no better introduction to their misty magic than Strawberry Hill.

Set on a former coffee plantation just 10 miles above Kingston, the hilltop retreat is the go-to hotel in the Blue Mountains. A trip here begins with a steep, 45-minute drive up from the city (the hairpin turns and winding rainforest roads are part of the fun), but it really kicks off once you take in the sweeping panoramas from the top. The 26-acre property is centered around a sleek infinity pool that overlooks Kingston and the Caribbean Sea. The pool area feels especially glamorous at night, thanks to the city’s twinkling lights in the distance and the sound of clinking silverware from the on-site restaurant (get the rum cake for dessert). All 12 Georgian-style cottages and villas also have verandas that overlook the mountains and gardens. And for the birders among us, Strawberry Hill is home to 24 endemic species of our favorite friends, including the Doctor Bird, the country’s national bird.

But the biggest allure may just be the music history. Island Records founder Chris Blackwell purchased Strawberry Hill in 1974, and his influence is felt throughout the hotel, from the gold and platinum records on the walls to the vintage black-and-white photos of Bob Marley and other artists (Marley actually recovered at Strawberry Hill after he was shot in 1976, and his time there famously inspired him to write “Natural Mystic” later on). My husband and I loved sitting at the bar with a Blackwell Rum Punch, naturally, and chatting with the bartender about all the other musicians who’ve stayed there through the years: Peter Tosh, Yoko Ono, Mick Jagger, and many more.

Amenities: infinity pool, mountainside spa, yoga pavilion, on-site restaurant, landscaped gardens, bar with a fireplace and vintage piano, hiking trails

Bonus tip: Order a pot of Blue Mountain coffee to your room each morning, and enjoy it on your veranda while soaking in the strong morning sun. There’s something about drinking Blue Mountain coffee straight from the source that just hits different.

Address: New Castle Road, Irish Town, St. Andrew

For those immersed in the Jamaican hotel scene, GoldenEye needs no introduction. The legendary property on Jamaica’s north coast is filled with lore, starting with its origin as James Bond author Ian Fleming’s private retreat, which he built in 1946. Today, the property is owned by none other than Island Records founder Chris Blackwell, who bought it in 1976 and later made it part of his Island Outpost portfolio (along with Strawberry Hill and The Caves in Negril).

Glitzy history aside, it would be hard to have a bad time at GoldenEye. The property is practically set up to lower your cortisol, with 45 accommodations spread across 52 acres that include lush tropical gardens, quiet beaches, and its star attraction: a protected lagoon. Whether you opt for a lagoon cottage with a private dock, a beach villa right on the sand, or Fleming’s villa itself (a splurge, to be sure), there is truly no bad option here. Guests can even kayak across the lagoon to their spa appointments.

Amenities: swimmable lagoon, two freshwater swimming pools, saltwater splash pool, spa, boutique, private beaches, tennis court, pickleball court, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, Sunfish and Hobie Cat sailboats, two on-site restaurants, one on-site bar

Bonus tip: Be sure to spend time at Bizot Bar, GoldenEye’s casual beach restaurant named after the late counter-cultural journalist Jean-François Bizot (who was good friends with Blackwell). The breezy soundtrack comes courtesy of Radio Nova, a Paris-based radio station founded by Bizot that plays an eclectic mix of world music.

Address: Race Course, Oracabessa, St. Mary

Owned and operated by the Morrow family for nearly 70 years, Jamaica Inn is filled with family traditions, like a succession of pet black labradors all named Shadow (the first Shadow dates back to the 1970s). The beach bar, Teddy’s, is named after longtime bartender Teddy Tucker, who joined in 1958. Many of the staffers have worked there for more than 30 years, and notable guests include Marilyn Monroe, Katharine Hepburn, and Winston Churchill.

All history aside, the hotel is also just a beautiful spot that lends itself to a properly lazy time. Located in Ocho Rios, a resort town on Jamaica’s north coast, it’s spread along a private beach often considered to be one of the best in the Caribbean, with 700 feet of soft golden sand and pristine turquoise waters. On top of that, all 55 suites, cottages, and beachfront bungalows have direct views of those waters—and many have private plunge pools as well. They even have a no-screen rule, meaning there aren’t any TVs, radios, or clocks in the rooms to remind you of life outside your seaside bubble (whether or not you choose to surrender your phone to that rule is up to you). If you can manage to pry yourself away from the “beach-eat-repeat” lifestyle, Jamaica Inn has an array of activities to explore, from James Bond film showings on the sand to a tour of the hotel’s cannabis farm partner, Jacana, which includes a lesson on the history of Rasta culture.

Amenities: outdoor pool, spa, croquet lawn, garden tours, daily afternoon tea presentation, yoga pavilion, library, boutique, fitness center, complimentary daily activities, nightly live music

Bonus tip: Music lovers must take a field trip to nearby Nine Mile, the birthplace of Bob Marley.

DJ and music producer Diplo once told Vogue that his personal style is “kind of random; it does whatever.” But judging from his private (yet rentable) retreat, Pompey, his design style is far more considered. Set on 62 acres of private land in lush Port Antonio, the eight-suite property—which opened in 2024—is more like a Brutalist creative compound than a hotel, one where everything is intentionally set up to help you channel Jamaica’s artistic spirit. There’s a recording studio, naturally, complete with professional gear, and an impressive list of extras, from ping pong and chess to a wet bar with stocked snacks and an outdoor wooden deck overlooking the rainforest. There’s also an outdoor yoga pavilion, an equestrian center, and a two-floor gym with wellness facilities including hydrotherapy, infrared sauna, and skincare treatments with products from the legendary Dr. Barbara Sturm. All stays come fully staffed with daily housekeeping and a full-time chef, who, instead of supplying menus, cooks based on the vibe of the day.

Designed by Brooklyn studio Freecell Architecture and architect Gia Wolff, the concrete retreat is meant to both blend into nature and look striking against it. Centered around a saltwater infinity pool, the property stretches out into a regenerative farm and orchard with all sorts of walking paths, ATV trails, and direct access to Port Antonio’s beautiful San San Beach. Even if you’re not blessed with a productive burst of creativity while you’re there, you’ll likely still leave feeling relaxed and at peace—a win, either way.

Amenities: recording studio, on-property helicopter access, saltwater infinity pool, yoga pavilion, gym, equestrian center, ATV access, E-bikes, walking paths, regenerative farm and orchard, concierge-led programming

Bonus tip: To book, email Pompey’s concierge directly through their website. Rooming configurations are quite flexible, so tell them exactly what you’re looking for and they will set you up accordingly—they can even arrange additional accommodations five minutes away for larger groups.

Address: Fairy Hill, Port Antonio, Portland

Mention Treasure Beach to anyone familiar with Jamaica, and they will likely think of Jakes. Since its opening in 1993, the 60-room boutique hotel has become something of a treasure in Treasure Beach—pun very much intended—and it’s not hard to see why. Founded by Jamaica-born artist and designer Sally Henzell, Jakes reflects her creative sensibility everywhere you look. The bungalows, cottages, villages and rooms are painted in a rainbow of colors, and they’re all decorated with local art. Like most of Jamaica’s south coast, Jakes was hit hard by Hurricane Melissa last year, but fortunately, it began welcoming guests again that December and fully reopened in March with reimagined oceanfront bungalows. Its whimsical design is still a big part of the appeal.

The other main appeal? Treasure Beach itself. Unlike some of Jamaica’s more tourism-oriented hubs like Montego Bay and Ocho Rios, Treasure Beach is quite low-key. There are a few guesthouses and restaurants, but mostly it’s just rocky coastline, houses that dot the fields, and splashes of magenta bougainvillea. No all-inclusives, no cruise ships. For book lovers, the property hosts the Calabash International Literary Festival every other May. It’s drawn a glittery crowd over the years, from authors (Zadie Smith, Marlon James, and Padma Lakshmi, to name a few) to guests including Angelina Jolie.

Amenities: private beach and dock, freshwater pool, three restaurants, ocean-facing spa, seaside yoga deck with daily sessions, gift shop, monthly full moon dinners, on-site art classes

Bonus tip: Take the complimentary boat trip to Floyd’s Pelican Bar, Treasure Beach’s iconic thatched-roof bar that sits on stilts in the middle of the sea. It was fully destroyed by Hurricane Melissa, but has since reopened.

Address: Calabash Bay, Treasure Beach, Saint Elizabeth

While Montego Bay has its fair share of standard all-inclusives, Round Hill is anything but. Set on 110 lush acres of former pineapple groves, the storied boutique has been the go-to spot for an elegant stay in the area since it opened in 1953. John F. Kennedy and Jackie Kennedy honeymooned there, and Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have visited, too. But no guest is more associated with the property than Ralph Lauren. He visited for the first time at Christmas in 1978 and loved it so much, he proceeded to buy two cottages there: High Rock in 1982, and White Orchid in 1996. In the early 2000s, Lauren even redesigned all 36 rooms in the main hotel (known as the Pineapple House), as well as the cocktail lounge, which is considered to be the original Polo Bar. His touch is evident in the country club style that runs throughout: white stone floors, four-poster mahogany bamboo beds, and the green-and-white striped awnings.

Aside from those 36 Pineapple House rooms Lauren designed, there are also 27 individually-owned villas, ranging from two to six bedrooms. Travelers also book Round Hill for its impeccable landscaping and fresh feel. It’s an extremely well-manicured resort, after all—one where lush gardens seem to stretch on for miles and open skies are never hard to find. Add an array of activities to the mix—including tennis, pickleball, and river rafting—plus island fare from the property’s 11 dining options, and you’ve got everything you need for an idyllic tropical stay.

Amenities: spa, fitness center and fitness classes, outdoor infinity pool, walking trail, water sports facility, house reef, boutique, chef’s garden, events pavilion, daily complimentary afternoon tea, nightly entertainment

Bonus tip: During the festive season, Round Hill hosts daily cocktail classes at 3 p.m., where you can learn about the history of Jamaican rum and Blue Mountain coffee—and make your own cocktails, of course.

Address: John Pringle Drive, Montego Bay, Hanover

Set on 400 acres along two miles of Montego Bay coastline, Half Moon has been a resort mainstay on Jamaica’s north shore since it opened in 1954. It’s known for its whitewashed cottages, wide verandas, and unmistakably grand feel. JFK stayed there (the man clearly loved Jamaica!), as did many members of the British royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II, then-Prince Charles, and Prince Harry. Sadly, because Half Moon is quite open to the elements, it was hit especially hard by Hurricane Melissa last year, which caused extensive damage to the property and personally affected more than 850 of its team members. Some villas reopened in April after a major restoration effort, but the historic resort just announced that most of the remaining property will reopen by Thanksgiving, followed by the final batch of cottages by the festive season. That includes a mix of rebuilds, redesigns, and new additions like Garlandstone Gallery, which will sell local art.

Half Moon is particularly strong in the tropical activity department: golf, tennis, pickleball, water sports, locally inspired spa treatments, and excursions that go deeper into Jamaican culture are all available. I especially loved the farm-to-table vegan dining experience at Stush in the Bush, an organic farm and restaurant in the lush fields of St. Ann. Think crispy plantain chips, wood-fired pizza, and skillet cornbread, all served with herbs from the garden and their own line of gourmet sauces and spreads.

Amenities: private beach, infinity pool, swimming coves and lagoon, spa, golf course, equestrian center, tennis and pickleball courts, water sports, sailing and diving classes, sea turtle releases, on-site garden, fitness studio, 10 bars and restaurants, children’s village

Bonus tip: The hotel’s collection of paintings from Montego Bay artist Michael Lester is now available for purchase. Lester, who died in 1972, is known for his expressionist paintings of Montego Bay and Jamaican life.

Address: Rose Hall, Montego Bay, St. James

Plus, the cabin itself is incredibly peaceful. With a lush garden filled with birds, plants scattered throughout the home, and exposed cedar beams in most rooms, it feels like a true city oasis. Perhaps best of all? The cabin is located directly under a mango tree, so you get a real taste of island living. (The owner, Terryon, may even greet you with a fresh mango smoothie.)

Amenities: Outdoor shower, HDTV, AC, backyard, outdoor dining furniture, hammock, free parking

If you’re looking for the perfect spot for a tropical group getaway, say for a birthday or a bachelorette, look no further than this massive Airbnb in Negril. Set beneath a grove of palm trees just steps from the famed Seven Mile Beach, it sleeps up to ten people and comes fully staffed with a private chef, butler, and housekeeper. There’s a gorgeous pool with loungers, and a large outdoor dining table perfect for long group dinners.

All five bedrooms come equipped with a four-poster king bed, private bathroom, private terrace, and ocean views—here, there is no surrendering to the “bad room” just to make someone else happy. There are also multiple hangout rooms for lounging, all with an airy, white-on-wood tropical design and colorful artwork on the walls. Reviewers are especially into the butler service, with one saying her butler would just “appear at the beach” with a carafe of hot coffee anytime hers was running low (Jamaican hospitality at its finest). And to really take any possible friction out of your group stay, you can even arrange for the kitchen to come pre-stocked at an additional cost.

Amenities: Chef and cleaning available during stay, pool, AC, washer, TV, bar, outdoor furniture, beachfront access, kayak, free parking

Alaska was finally called for Mary Peltola. I sure hope Hakeem Jeffries, the soon-to-be Speaker of the House, knows what to do with his majority.

I rather like these extended post-election activities. Every few days, another seat in Congress flips from R to D, and all the joy and wonder comes flooding back again. Up in Alaska, Democratic candidate Mary Peltola was (finally) declared the winner of the Senate race. She also managed to clear the 50 percent mark, which means that the race didn't have to go into the land of Ranked Choice voting, which would have resulted in Republicans birthing bovines all over Alaska and the Lower 48.

For the record, Peltola's total votes exceeded those of both Dan Sullivans combined. Whoever deployed the JFK strategy failed against the power of fish, family, and freedom. And, truth be told, Peltola, thus far, has been a committed Blue Dog. In her one term in the House, she was one of the strongest Democratic supporters of some conservative immigration policies. She also lined up against Washington, D.C.'s independence in sentencing criminals. But, big tent and all of that.

Meanwhile, in Washington, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries easily won the endorsement of the Democratic caucus to be the next Speaker. It was particularly easy because there were no other candidates. From The New York Times:

The question remains open as to whether Jeffries—and, to a more critical extent, Senator Chuck Schumer—recognize the power they've been given by the midterm elections, a necessary precondition to putting that power to actual use. The iron will never be hotter.

#6729. Shop Sienna Miller’s Best Off-Duty Fall Outfits

Sienna Miller has never been one to shy away from a statement look, but lately the actress has taken a noticeably more understated approach to getting dressed. As we await the gripping conclusion of HBO’s War this Thursday, we’re taking a closer look at the actress’s off-duty style over the past few weeks—and we noticed one thing in particular: Each look was anchored by a great piece of outerwear.

Rather than the flowing silhouettes and eclectic layering the perennial boho girl has been known for in the past, she’s leaning into wardrobe foundations with a minimalist sensibility this season—perhaps taking a cue from her War character, Carla Duval, and her pared-back closet. Her recent roster includes bomber jackets, tailored coats, and leather motos, among other staples—but don’t mistake these for predictable basics. There’s a peplum-waist leather jacket with a more sculptural shape, a zip-up blouson in a bold shade of red, and even a trench coat updated in brown corduroy. Each one brings something unexpected to the otherwise classic fall lineup.

Her styling approach is equally unfussy, keeping the focus on the outerwear itself and pairing each piece with everyday essentials. Think black pleated trousers, lived-in denim, simple T-shirts, and cozy knitwear. Accessories follow the same less-is-more philosophy, from a strappy heel she's worn on repeat in two different colorways to a timeless designer tote and understated jewelry. It’s proof that the best fall outfits don’t have to be complicated—but they should always start with a really good jacket.

Ahead, find easy fall outfit formulas inspired by Sienna Miller’s style.

Sienna Miller leaned into the peplum leather jacket trend with Balmain’s sculptural take—a feminine twist on the classic moto shape. She kept the rest of the look simple with a black top, tailored trousers, and strappy sandals—which can easily be swapped for pointy ankle boots as temperatures continue to drop. Consider this a masterclass in giving the all-black outfit a little more personality.

A pop of red is the enduring color trend that the fashion crowd can’t quit—and a zip-up jacket is the easiest way to wear it. Miller styled hers effortlessly over a navy crewneck sweater and frayed white jeans, finishing the look with her favorite high-vamp black flats, Gucci’s Ophidia tote, and a printed scarf around the neck. It’s especially on point for transitional dressing or a polished travel outfit.

Minimalist ’90s-style coats are everywhere—perhaps as a byproduct of the Love Story effect that swept the fashion conversation earlier this year. Miller put her own spin on the classic piece, wearing it with a crisp blue button-down and pleated trousers, then adding strappy red Jude heels—a style she’s been wearing on repeat lately. Add a structured top-handle bag and gold chain necklace to complete the everyday look, perfect for the office and beyond.

Trench coats are something of a British wardrobe institution, but Miller gave the heritage silhouette a fresh spin in brown corduroy. Underneath, she kept things understated, styling a simple black top with a pleated plaid skirt and knee-high boots. Add a waist belt and shoulder bag to carry the look through the day—a timeless fall outfit you’ll return to over and over.

Transitional dressing is all about the layers—and Sienna Miller has the off-duty formula down. A khaki bomber jacket, white T-shirt, and relaxed denim make up the foundation, while a navy knit tossed over the shoulders adds an extra layer for cooler mornings or evenings. Finish with her go-to red strappy heels for a little contrast or swap in ballet flats for an equally easy daytime option.

#6727. Do Monsters Lurk Around Us in Plain Sight? Gentle Monster’s Director Worries They Do

Bazaar spoke with Austrian director Marie Kreutzer about her Cannes favorite starring Léa Seydoux and Laurence Rupp

A newspaper clipping about a ring of pedophiles captivated the attention of Austrian filmmaker Marie Kreutzer one morning six years ago. The article detailed the buildup and the arrest in explicit detail, but one description felt more haunting than the rest.

“It was shocking because most of the guys in that ring of criminals were normal family dads,” Kreutzer tells Bazaar on a recent call. “It made me so much more aware of how close these perpetrators are, more than we want to think, and that I must almost certainly also know one.… When I read that article, and it described how the police officers were standing at the doorsteps of these guys, my first thought was, ‘How would that be for me if it were my husband?’ ”

Kreutzer decided to channel this shock, the all-consuming fear that we cannot trust those we love the most, into her latest film, Gentle Monster. Releasing on Netflix on November 18, the film tells the story of Lucy Weiss (Léa Seydoux), an experimental pianist who leaves her life behind to raise her young son with her doe-eyed husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp). The trio exists happily in the German countryside, complete with all the comforts of a cozy domestic life. Lucy and Philip love each other and their son, enjoying a sex-filled marriage that appears to have only the regular bumps. This illusion is disrupted when police knock on the door, arresting Philip for his alleged participation in a child pornography ring. Kruetzer designed the couple introduction to feel as if the rug were pulled out from under the viewer.

“It was obviously very important to have all these scenes where they interact before everything happens and where we see that they have a very natural, loving relationship,” she says. “For me, [Rupp] has nothing secretive or mysterious about him. He’s very there. And that’s what I wanted for the role, because I thought it would be good to see him and never really be open to believing that that guy would really do something like that.” She remembered telling Rupp, “It’s not like you’re playing a petty criminal. You’re playing a liar.” Kruetzer wanted him to “make us want to come back to you.”

In this way, Rupp embodies an uncanny confidence throughout the entire movie. He, of course, carries a sense of guilt, yet an audience can’t easily parse out the weight of his internal feelings. Kruetzer also refrains from giving too much direction about his innocence or guilt. Even when he is released from prison the first time, his nonchalance diffuses any skepticism; you might believe him when he says he has nothing to do with it. And when evidence mounts, including actual files, he twists the story again, telling Lucy he did it for the money. Rupp’s sympathetic portrayal is confusing—enough so that you can understand Lucy’s turmoil. Kruetzer remembers telling him to “play it as if you just messed up the taxes,” and later he told her, “I didn’t really play the monster; I played the gentle.”

This portrayal adds weight to Seydoux’s indelible performance as Lucy. The entire film orbits her reaction to this horrific revelation. Seydoux’s anger and forgiveness oscillate at a frenetic pace throughout the movie, pulling the viewer into Lucy’s point of view, as well as what Kreutzer first felt when she read the newspaper clipping.

Casting Seydoux, the director says, felt intuitive. The French actress dove headfirst into the script, expressing great interest in the character and the story. “The subject matter is tough, but the fact that it’s through the woman’s perspective—and not through the victim or perpetrator—it’s through her emotions that the story unfolds [is what interested me],” Seydoux says in Bazaar’s profile from last week. One bone-rattling scene in particular, where Lucy faces off with Philip in a light rain and directly confronts him about his arrest, underscores why she’s considered one of the best living French actresses. “As soon as we turned the camera towards her, it was really surprising what came out of her and what poured out of her,” Kreutzer said. “I remember that the crew was in shock.”

The main storyline provides enough anxiety and suspense, yet Kreutzer wrote a side plot for Gentle Monster to offer perspective. One of the cops who knocks on the Weiss family door, Elsa (Jella Haase), provides a removed point of view on Lucy’s internal dilemma. The character provides a broader understanding of the crime at the center of this story, emphasizing how widespread and hidden this problem is. “For Lucy, her life is falling apart because of this, whereas for Elsa, it’s just one of many cases, and it’s not even a bad one,” Kreutzer says. “It was important for me to show the magnitude of the problem and to not let the audience lean back and think, ‘Okay, that’s very dramatic, but it has nothing to do with me.’ ”
