#6726. The Fearless Sensitivity of ‘Mouse’ and ‘Clarissa’ Star Sophie Okonedo

Sophie Okonedo is one of those performers whose very presence can make a scene feel more alive. The Tony Award–winning British actor projects both warmth and watchfulness, moving swiftly from humor to hurt, or authority to vulnerability, without announcing the shift. Even in a supporting role, she has a way of making you lean in.

This winter she leads two independent features opening theatrically after an international festival run: Clarissa, by brothers Chuko and Arie Esiri, and Mouse, by husband-and-wife team Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Though shot nearly a year apart, the two films are arriving within weeks of each other—a quirk of the release calendar that makes for an unusually timely double feature.

Mouse, out now, is a coming-of-age story set in 2002 Arkansas, in which the teenage Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) develops a complicated relationship with her best friend’s mother (Okonedo) after an unexpected tragedy. Meanwhile, Clarissa—in limited theaters December 18—transposes Virginia Woolf’s novel Mrs. Dalloway to contemporary Nigeria, a project that brought Okonedo to a country she hadn’t visited in two decades. (Her late father, whom she was mostly estranged from, moved back to his home country when she was young.)

Filming in Lagos proved consequential in ways that extended well beyond the work itself. “The journey I had in Lagos was so immense, personally and professionally, that I remember thinking on the wrap day that even if nothing else happens with this film, I’ve already gotten everything I wanted,” she tells Vogue.

Both films were made on tiny budgets, and as Okonedo points out, a conversation about one inevitably opens up a conversation about the other. So we talked about both.

Vogue: Let’s start with Mouse. How did it come to you? What was it about your character, Helen, or about the directors that made you say yes?

Sophie Okonedo: I didn’t read anything about them. I read the script completely cold. By the time I got to the end, I rang my agent and said, “I’m absolutely doing this. I don’t know who’s directing, I don’t know what’s happening with the film, but I’m doing it.” So he sent me their last film, Ghostlight. It’s such a brilliant film, and it was made for pennies. These are two really interesting filmmakers who are talking about America in a way I haven’t seen—very quietly. There are no explosions, no big movie stars, and it’s deeply significant. Kelly’s writing is subtle and real. But films like this can slip by without anyone noticing. I have to galvanize everyone and get them behind it because I think it’s so good.

Helen ends up mothering her daughter’s friend, Minnie, in a way that’s unnerving at times, as if she’s grieving and replacing her at the same time.

It’s totally inappropriate at times. She even says it at one point: “Oh my God, I’m the adult here.” She uses Minnie to ease her own grief, then backtracks, then moves forward again. It’s a messy situation, but there’s hope in it. The film is funny too. Kelly has that gift for finding levity in dark situations. But they never get you to play the comedy. You play the seriousness of it all, and it’s funny as it goes along.

I realized after watching the film that the woman playing Katherine’s mother is her real-life mother. What was that dynamic like on set?

She wasn’t even meant to play the part at first. Tara [Mallen], her mother, is a theater actress. She runs a theater company in Chicago and was there as Katherine’s guardian. They’d cast a great local actor, but on the first day we realized it wasn’t right. By the second day, Tara stepped in. Everything was so homegrown. My baby in the film is actually Kelly and Alex’s baby. They removed all the blockers you normally have as an actor on a film, where you spend three hours in hair and makeup. Sometimes you need those things, but this film didn’t. You just rock up and start filming. It was very seamless.

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo in Mouse

You shot on location in North Little Rock. Had you been to Arkansas before?

Never. I got there a little early to check it out because I was playing an outsider but an outsider who’d lived there for 15 years. So I had to know the place and feel familiar with it. All the locations came from [O’Sullivan’s] childhood. You could ask her, “What happened here?” and she’d tell you. Many people with small parts in the film knew Kelly from high school and were now playing mothers. The dance we see at the memorial was one Kelly actually performed herself. We even brought back the dance teacher who taught her so she could teach it to the two girls in the film.

Does playing an outsider give you something to work with? You didn’t do the method thing, keeping yourself apart from everyone, right?

No. I totally get that some people do, but I’m too shy to stay in character! I feel too silly. What I do is think very deeply about every single word I say in the script before I arrive. Because I’m theater trained, the script is my bible. All answers will be there. I spend a long time thinking about everything I say and everything everyone else says, and I go through it many, many times. An internal world builds up inside me. I can’t really explain how it happens. When I get to set, I forget any notes or journals I’ve made. I drop it all, empty myself, and see what happens. I feel buoyant and flexible, not stuck in any particular way.

Mouse is so specific about 2002, down to the Michelle Branch music cues. I was a bit younger than the characters then, but it all felt right. What did setting it in that moment bring to the story?

I’m older, but Kelly was that age in 2002, so she had all the references. She knew exactly what she was listening to, what she was thinking and feeling. The main difference is there were no cell phones back then. If you wanted information, it had to come to you through someone taking action. The jogger has to tell Minnie something, then she has to run to the house to see if it’s really happened, then she has to look for a phone book. Now it would just be someone posting “RIP Callie” on Instagram. It’s so much more interesting to film people taking an action than all these constant shots of phones and texts, which I see in movies all the time now. It’s so boring.

In Mouse, Helen and Minnie come from very different backgrounds. Class is also woven into Clarissa, where you play the titular role. Was that a connection you were conscious of while working on the two films?

Class is massive in Britain. We live and breathe it. It runs through every vein of everyone’s body here, probably more than anything else, so I’m very aware of it. But there’s another weird parallel between the films: Mouse is directed by a couple, and one of them is the writer. Clarissa is directed by two brothers, and one of them is the writer. With both, I had an instant, visceral response. I didn’t need to think about the whys and wherefores. It was just yes, yes, yes. With a lot of other work, I have to get myself into the right position or work it out. What’s also amazing is that the scripts for Clarissa and Mouse barely changed between that first draft and the start of filming—the same was true of Janet Planet. These are filmmakers who have thought deeply about what they’re writing. There weren’t a million drafts or endless revisions; all three films were already in a remarkably evolved state from the start. Even though Mouse looks improvised in places, I’m sticking to the script.

But parts of Mouse were improvised, right? I’m thinking of the scene where Helen attends a grief group.

It was a real grief group. I knew the man handing me coffee at the beginning was an actor, though by coincidence he was also in a grief group. I was just outside the room; they put two cameras in there, and someone called action. I walked in, and during the scene it slowly dawned on me—someone had forgotten to tell me these weren’t actors!

The scene is short, but that take lasted an hour and 10 minutes—the exact length of the group. If it were scripted, I probably would have talked and broken down. But I couldn’t speak; their stories were so extraordinary. I kept talking to them afterward, thinking the cameras had stopped, until I realized they were still filming. Alex will do that. You don’t even know. There’s no “cut.”

Both films are concerned with motherhood, though in very different ways. In Mouse, there’s an absent daughter; in Clarissa, she keeps her living daughter at arm’s length. Did these characters speak to each other in any way?

It’s a good question, because I find that when I do a part, it usually feeds into the next one. The next role I played after Clarissa was Natalya in Turgenev’s A Month in the Country, in London. She’s a woman of a certain age looking back, wondering whether she made the right choices, and she has a very separate relationship with her son. I was thinking that a lot of Clarissa was in her.

I read that Arie and Chuko drew on their own mother in shaping the film and that you got to spend time with her. How did that influence your performance?

When they cast me, I wondered if I could do this. I told them I didn’t recognize the Lagos in the script and that I had such a fractured relationship with the country. They said, “If nothing else, we’ll bridge that for you.” That meant a lot. Before filming, Chuko invited me to stay with him and his mother. I ended up staying the whole shoot and got very close to her. I used her a lot, more than she realizes, perhaps. Like Clarissa, she employs staff [in her home], and I observed how she interacted with them. I didn’t want to turn her into a caricature out of Downton Abbey. You can just be real with them, the way she was.

You also just don’t see stories like this coming out of Africa, and I say that broadly. The subject matter is usually very narrow: Africa is depicted as war-torn, impoverished. Here was a film about people. There’s a backdrop of war and social and economic circumstances, but that isn’t the main thrust. I long to see films where we as Africans, as Nigerians, get every part of ourselves represented, just as our white Western counterparts get films about everything. It’s the same with queer films and Black films: They shouldn’t only be about being queer or Black. That shouldn’t have to be the whole story.

And on top of that, Clarissa is character driven and not plot driven.

The thought of going to Lagos and making an arthouse film on 35 millimeter was incredible. It’s an impossible book to film. People have tried many times, and mostly it doesn’t work. I was taking a punt. I just wanted to be part of it. I hardly say anything but say a million words with my face.

What is it like to project that kind of interiority? It’s sort of a paradox: Clarissa is deep in thought, but she also doesn’t let you in much.

She’s hard to read, but you have to make her really easy to read for the camera. She’s protective, but you have to let the camera in. I didn’t think about it that deeply. I just have that sort of face. I’m really sensitive, hypersensitive, which is so difficult in my normal life, but it’s great for acting. My grandmother used to say, “Your face changes like the wind.” Everything shows. Chuko or Arie would only have to whisper the slightest thing in my ear, and it would show.

People always say to watch an actor’s eyes, but I noticed so much happens in the lower half of your face. It holds everything.

That’s why I could never do any of that stuff to my face. I’d be too frightened! I know I only have to think the glimmer of a thought and it’ll show. I don’t know what happens to my face because I don’t really watch myself, but doing something that would stop that would be the end of my career.

The story famously centers on your character throwing a party. Are you more of a host or a guest?

I’m quite a good host, actually. I don’t do it often because I go overboard and it’s exhausting. I love cooking and making lovely things. I used to spend the whole time panicking in the kitchen, but I’ve learned it doesn’t really matter what you serve. It’s about how you engage with guests. They just want you to be part of the party.

Did you watch any of the other adaptations of Mrs. Dalloway to prepare for Clarissa?

I watched about three minutes of one with Vanessa Redgrave and realized we’re not doing this type of film, so I didn’t carry on. Chuko and Arie would have watched everything, though. They’re complete cinephiles.

Did they give you suggestions on films to watch to prepare then?

They probably did, but I forgot because my brain is a sieve. They gave up on me. They’d mention really famous films, and I’d say I hadn’t seen them. I don’t know what I do with my time. I don’t fill it wisely. I just seem to mess around most of the day, and then it’s gone!

It sounds like you’re living your own stories instead of watching other people’s on screen.

You’re putting it nicely. As my husband says, I spend a lot of time daydreaming. I’ve got a really nice view. [Turns her laptop to the window to show the view.] I spend a lot of time just looking out at the trees with my dog.

After this double-header year, what are you looking for next?

Because I’m getting older, I don’t see an eternity stretching out in front of me anymore, and I find myself asking how I want to spend my time. I’ve decided that my heart is really in independent films and theater, so I’m going to wait until the right thing comes along. You might find me still unemployed a year from now. Nothing has come up yet that’s been worth getting on a plane for.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6723. Stylist and Creative Director Akari Endo-Gaut’s Guide to Tokyo

Perhaps no city juggles the past and the future as nimbly as Tokyo. Sleek skyscrapers meet centuries-old shrines; a rich culinary tradition blends with contemporary innovation (it’s no accident that this is the city with the most Michelin starred-restaurants in the world). The fashion, of course, exists in a similar dichotomy, expertly blending traditional techniques with the avant-garde. There’s never a wrong time to visit the Japanese capital—but in winter, when ski resorts a quick day trip away are in full swing and New Year’s celebrations are on the horizon, it feels particularly special. All you have to do is narrow down your itinerary.

In fact, there’s so much to discover that you could spend an entire trip dedicated to shopping alone—according to Akari Endo-Gaut, a Japan-born, New York-based stylist and creative director who studied in Tokyo, it may be worth bringing a second suitcase just for souvenirs. From the vintage shops to put on your radar to the best place to stop for a glass of natural wine, here’s a glimpse at Endo-Gaut’s Tokyo little black book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Since I was student in Tokyo, one of my favorite areas to hang around was Minami-Aoyama. We used to have amazing Corso Como store there; now, the Comme des Garçons store, the Issey Miyake Pleats Please shop, and the Auralee store there are still where you can go to find a special piece.

For vintage gems: There are so many good vintage shops in Tokyo, and it goes deep. BerBer Jin is always my first stop, and I also check luxury resale shops like Komehyo.

For unique souvenirs: You can find the best curated products, from ceramic bowls to German knives, at Arts and Science. And beautifully wrapped sweets at Higashiya are the best gifts.

For a worthwhile investment piece: Wako Arts and Culture is a new space conceived by artist Hiroshi Sugimoto in the basement of a prestigious department store in Ginza. It’s all specially curated, a great spot to find a special piece from fashion to Japanese craft.

For the magpie: My very talented friend Charlotte Chesnais from Paris recently opened a shop in Tokyo; it’s a must-visit. Or, if you’re looking for best-condition vintage watches, you can go to ECW Shoto.

For your next great read: Japan has a big book culture—go to Komiyama bookstore for vintage books, or spend a full weekend browsing at Tsutaya Daikanyama or SKAC.

For stylish home goods: You can find traditional but beautiful kitchen goods at Kiya and, of course, at Muji. Or, spend a fun day exploring all the kitchen goods stores in the Kappabashi area, which is a shopping street dedicated to restaurant owners.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Hakujitsu houses a beautiful collection of ceramics in an old dentist building. My secret favorite is Yanaka Matsunoya—it has the best baskets and tote bags.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Japanese-Chinese food or yakiniku, so I go to Chugoku Hanten with local friends or to Jojoen with my sister. If I have foreign guests, they usually have fun dining experience at Narukiyo.

For a bakery treat: Sawamura is our best local bakery cafe in Hiroo. After a soba lunch at Kanda, stop by Omiya Western Sweets Shop for the cutest pastry; for traditional Japanese sweets at an upscale, architecturally beautiful spot, go to Toraya Akasaka.

For the art-lover: Taka Ishii and Tomio Koyama are the best fine arts galleries in Tokyo. I like the artists from Kosaku Kanechika too, and at Licht gallery, you can see the best design pieces.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: For the architecture lover, a drink at Imperial Bar, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, is a must. When I’m hanging out with local friends, I’d go for a natural wine at Le Cabaret or Tabac.

For your packing list: Honestly, you don’t need anything, since you go to Tokyo to buy the best of all items! Bring flat shoes for walking, and an extra suitcase for shopping. An eye mask and melatonin for the 13-hour time difference will come in handy, as will a handkerchief; it’s part of local etiquette to carry one. And I always like to bring a running outfit for the famous Imperial Palace run.

#6721. Best Harrington Jackets 2026: Preppy, Punk, and Ultra-Functional

Few jackets have managed to cross as many style tribes—and decades—as the Harrington. In fact, if you were to enroll in Classic Menswear 101, the Harrington jacket would be a prerequisite. The transitional season staple—a favorite of Elvis, James Dean, Steve McQueen, and every member of The Clash—is constantly found across lookbooks and style Instagram accounts, because it does so many things so well.

For one, it's incredibly practical: Water-resistant, pocket-forward, lightly insulating, and ever-adaptable to the day's conditions thanks to its full-zip and collar. But the almost-cropped length—and popped collar, if you so dare—is also a style swerve that makes every wearer feel one dose cooler than they did before. No wonder it’s been embraced over the decades by everyone from golfers to preppies to A-Listers and punks.

The original Harrington—a Baracuta G9—is still available almost a century on from its release, and still excellent. But if you’re looking to broaden your horizons, today’s Harrington jackets aren’t resting on their laurels. Below, the standout versions worth adding to your rotation before we’re into parka territory.

The classic Baracuta G9 golf jacket is as British as beans on toast. This is the original tartan-lined, ribbed-cuff Harrington, the jacket you picture when you think of Steve McQueen or Paul Newman, and the brand that insider-y menswear favorites like Engineered Garments and Noah have collaborated with when they wanted to make Harringtons of their own. Baracuta got its start making raincoats for other brands—Burberry included—before branching out with its own designs, and the G9 is still made in England today. Crafted from a water-resistant cotton-poly blend, and featuring the signature Fraser tartan lining and iconic umbrella back yoke (which keeps rain off your back while letting air circulate) it really doesn't get any better than this.

Uniqlo delivers a whole Harrington jacket without sacrificing anything, and in fact saves you some precious dollars along the way. We’re talking a slightly cropped, slightly relaxed silhouette, a touch of stretch, classic slant pockets and even a genre-affirming plaid lining. And while it’s not water-resistant like some other options, it makes up for it with a durable cotton fabric that’ll dry off in no time, and still keep you protected from a few unforeseen raindrops. If you’re after the workaday Harrington aesthetic without spending a lot, this one gets the job done and then some.

If you're looking to purchase a Harrington jacket that'll serve you for seasons to come, but don't particularly want to spend half your rent check on it, J.Crew's faithful take on the Harrington is as true as it gets. And this is no compromise pick: It still comes with plenty of details to get excited about, from the handsome, buttoned interior chest pocket to the warming full lining, leather zip tag, and 10-ounce cotton twill that's already been washed a few times by the brand to make it feel lived-in and well-loved from the jump. It also comes in multiple colors, partly because J.Crew is confident you'll be back for more. Oh, and if you want a winterized Harrington, check out the corduroy iteration, which also has a quilted, Primaloft-stuffed lining.

A pared-down, easygoing take on the classics, Quince’s Harrington strikes a smart balance of polished and sporty, without even the faintest fuss. Offered in khaki, navy and black, this one is the modern minimalist’s Harrington—a clean, contemporary style that does what a staple should do: make you look good without causing a scene. Oh, and that twill outer will break in wonderfully over time, in case you were wondering.

One of the best parts about a Harrington Jacket is that the idea is fully formed. As such, it can be a hard style to riff on, mostly because the source material is so dialed in that it’s often best to leave well enough alone. Ernest W. Baker designers Reid Baker and Inês Amorim, however, couldn’t care less about that tradition and went nuclear with this one: it’s a true-blue Harrington complete with a cropped fit, ribbing at the waist, barrel cuffs and a point collar. But then the inclusion of a leather collar and Western-inspired yoke details in lieu of the classic back vent turns it into something else entirely, without changing the fit one bit. And they nailed it. It’s transformative without being performative, utterly distinct and eminently familiar and, most improbably, contradiction free.

This has most of the trappings of your classic Harrington—stand collar, cool back vent, functional cuffs—but it also eschews the classic ribbed hem for a cinched waist, which adds a little bit of drama to the notoriously no-drama silhouette.

Todd Snyder often plays it straight—Ivy-ish classics with just the right details. Here, they’ve ditched part of the trad playbook and leaned into the modern with water-resistant tech cotton-nylon blend, but it's also a bit cropped and fits very much like you'd remember. And now, it's also on sale.

A Harrington is already pretty pared down, but Barbour trimmed every ounce of fat on this one, leaving us with a slightly longer silhouette, all the *essential* bells and whistles and a brown cotton outer that gets to take center stage.

We could get into the buttery leather collar or the insane Italian wool serge fabric that Wanze deployed on this stunner, or even lock in on that two-way RiRi zipper, but that'd be burying the lede because you're not going to get a red like this anywhere else.

We wouldn't typically include different versions of the same style in one guide, but when our Best Overall version also comes in a buttery suede, exceptions are made.

Stone Island traffics in the unexpected, so, in a way, it should come as no surprise that the Italian label's take on the classic is a Gonzo, teched-out one—one made with a garment-dyed fabric that's been treated with an "anti-drop" finish.

The Harrington is an icon of preppy style, so of course Ralph Lauren has blessed us with its lightweight cotton take, complete with the signature Polo pony on the chest. It’s preppy, American, and exactly the kind of jacket your kids will proudly say “This used to be my Dad’s” about.

You might not think of a Harrington as a "winter jacket," but hear us out: it can be. This Percival joint, for instance, is made out of a hardy birdseye wool blend that will hold up to some chilly weather and layer up nicely when calling things "chilly" is understatement.

The funniest thing about the Harrington? It wasn’t originally called a Harrington at all. The original—and, as you've read above, our favorite—was called the “G9.” It was cooked up by Baracuta in 1937 in rainy old Manchester, England, as a golf jacket—the “G” stands for “golf.” (The idea was to make a garment that could take a beating from British weather without cramping your backswing.) But the jacket earned its now-iconic name thanks to Rodney Harrington, a character from the 1960s TV show Peyton Place, who wore one so often that the name just stuck.

The traditional Harrington jacket fits close to the shoulders and chest, but still has enough room for a full range of arm motion—it is a golfing style, after all. The hem then typically sits either at the waist, or for a more stylized look, just above the belt line. It should be easy to spot from product shots whether the designer in question has stuck to this traditional shape, or elongated the style a touch. From that point, the only thing left to consider is whether you plan to wear it over thick sweaters, or lighter T-shirts and shirts. If it's the former, you may want to consider sizing up.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6718. Jewelry Designer Keri Ataumbi’s Guide to Santa Fe

Santa Fe is a perennial favorite for avid hikers and art lovers alike—but visit in winter, and you may just have some of its famed galleries and museums to yourself. Crowds thin out, skiers populate the trails, and glowing farolitos take over every public space. (Abiquiú, the onetime home of Georgia O’Keeffe where you can now visit her studio, is a short car trip away.) “Santa Fe has a lot of day hikes, lake trips, and soaks at the local hot springs,” says Keri Ataumbi, a Kiowa artist and fine jewelry designer based in town. You won’t run out of things to do on a winter trip out West; even the non-adventurer will find plenty to delight in.

It’s an excellent shopping destination, too: Santa Fe has a strong Native American artist tradition, and jewelry lovers especially will want to take note. We spoke to Ataumbi for all her best recommendations on where to find the best of it all—plus, a really good cocktail after a day of exploring it all. Just don’t forget the sunscreen; even in winter, the high altitude makes the UV glare intense.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: I’m a big fan of owning fewer, quality pieces that last. One of my current favorite tops came from Workshop and Wildlife; it’s an oversized, loose knit, hand-painted cashmere sweater by Avant Toi. Chocolate and Cashmere carries locally knit fine cashmere and locally made beautiful chocolates—I just bought one of their cozy serapes as a birthday present for myself last week. They have a large assortment of colors in the store.

For unique souvenirs: I think the best gifts are consumable, and Kakawa Chocolate House makes both beautiful and unusual chocolates. I love their elixirs, which range from historic pre-Columbian and old European recipes to contemporary creations.

For vintage gems: Double Take is great for treasure hunting, with everything from western boots and statement jewelry to vintage coats and kids’ clothing. Santa Fe Vintage is also fun, but it’s by appointment only.

For a worthwhile investment piece: I wear glasses everyday all day, so they are an essential part of how dress, and I’m an avid collector. Ojo Optique is locally owned and carries handcrafted frames you won’t find everywhere; plus, the owners are wonderful at choosing styles that flatter your face.

For the magpie: There’s so much amazing jewelry in Santa Fe! For Native American jewelry, I love Shiprock Santa Fe and the Case Trading Post. For something not Southwestern, The Golden Eye on Don Gaspar has been making high karat gold jewelry since 1971.

For your next great read: I just picked up a copy of American Bread by Andrew Coe at Garcia Street Books. Then I grabbed a coffee next door at Downtown Subscription and happily lost far too much time reading in their garden under the autumn sun.

For stylish home goods: For something special and unique, I head to the farm store, Los Poblanos Norte.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Take a day trip to Truchas to visit Eight Million Gods, where owner Heywood Simoneaux curates a perfectly eclectic store. Back in town, I love Gray Matter. On my last visit, they were unpacking medieval winemaking tools from a French museum; the Cooper’s adzes were my favorite.

For a bakery treat: I love everything at Dolina Bakery and Café, but the gingerbread tiles are my favorite. Owner Annamaria O’Brien is from Slovakia, so the locally sourced menu has Eastern European flavors.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: For a special dinner that’s still relaxed, I go to Izanami. It’s tucked into the mountains and serves small Japanese plates meant for sharing.

For the art-lover: Cara Romero Studio is a photography studio that also hosts group shows, run by my dear friend Cara, an internationally recognized Chemehuevi artist. Her work is deeply thoughtful, with beautifully saturated theatrical compositions.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: Last month when a friend visited from New York, we had gorgeous cocktails at As Above, So Below, a local distillery that uses local ingredients. Mine was made with fragrant juniper and piñon Sigil gin, butterfly pea flower tea, and a 24k gold garnish.

For your packing list: Do not forget a water bottle and electrolytes—it’s 7,000 feet and very dry, so staying hydrated helps with possible altitude sickness. I love Larroudé sneakers for practicality in Santa Fe, where there are a lot of rocky and uneven surfaces to traverse around town, and my go-to cotton travel trouser is a barrel-leg pair from Nili Lotan. The high desert is extremely dry, so I also recommend the piñon body oil, which is locally made from Dryland Wilds.

#6717. John Mulaney Wore Joe DiMaggio’s Watch to Host 'Saturday Night Live'

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Between sniffing out paternal autism and perfecting his Robert F. Kennedy impression, you may have noticed that John Mulaney was wearing an extraordinary watch while hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend. It’s a beauty—a gold vintage Patek Philippe with swoopy Breguet numerals—but its backstory is even more impressive. On December 12, 1948, New York Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio purchased this timepiece and owned it until his death in 1999.

The Patek Philippe, a ref. 130 circa 1947, is already a rare bird before you add in its Joltin’ Joe provenance. The model is one of just 180 made in yellow gold with Breguet numerals, and only 55 with this same combination have ever reached the secondary market. In late October, dealer Eric Wind of Wind Vintage put this specific watch up for sale with a $1.2 million asking price. “I think it’s the greatest Patek that’s known and tied to any athlete,” Wind told Robb Report last month.

For his seventh time hosting SNL, Mulaney came to Wind in search of “an important watch,” the dealer explains now. After surveying Wind’s entire catalog, the comedian landed on this piece, whose ties to a legendary New Yorker felt right for helming one of the city’s most hallowed institutions. To be clear, Mulaney only borrowed the watch for the show, which means its legend will have only grown by the time it reaches an eventual buyer. Talk about an illustrious provenance: A DiMaggio-owned Patek that also appeared on Saturday Night Live. “It was a very special moment and another cool moment of history for this important Patek Philippe,” Wind says.

As a known history buff and devoted baseball fan, the watch likely appealed to Mulaney on several levels. But its eggshell-hued dial also happened to go perfectly with the brown suit Mulaney sported during his opening monologue. “John has classic styling,” Wind says, “and the Joe DiMaggio Patek Philippe was the chef’s kiss on his wrist.”

Over the past several years, Mulaney has emerged as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and tasteful watch collectors. He is an eager and omnivorous admirer, bouncing between his beloved Rolex Air-King, loud Chopard chronographs, and glamorous Grand Seikos.

Mulaney, styled by Michael Fisher, wearing Cavour

During our watch-focused interview last May, Mulaney told me that he steers away from more obvious models like your garden-variety Rolex Submariner. “I don’t ask any questions about it, I know what it is,” he explained. “And I’m just more interested in watches that [are a little more] mysterious.” As an example, Mulaney specifically referenced a Patek Philippe Calatrava his wife Olivia Munn bought him.

The DiMaggio Patek is full of intrigue. The watch obviously has important provenance, but it’s historic on its own accord, too. The ref. 130 is named for the movement inside, known as the Calibre 130. That engine was the basis for Patek’s 1518, the first serially produced watch to combine a perpetual calendar and chronograph.

Funnily enough, this isn’t the first Mulaney, DiMaggio, and SNL crossover. In his 2018 special Kid Gorgeous at Radio City, the comedian explained what it was like working with famous SNL hosts during his time as a staff writer. “It’d be like if you went into your childhood bedroom and Joe DiMaggio was sitting there,” Mulaney quipped. “Yeah, he’s Joe DiMaggio, he’s a legend, he had sex with Marilyn Monroe, but only you know where the bathroom is.” And only Mulaney has had DiMaggio’s watch on his wrist, for now.

#6715. Classic Stuffing

While traditional stuffing is technically supposed to be stuffed inside the turkey to cook, that isn’t actually the ideal or even recommended way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or stuffing). I've found that you’ll achieve much better results by cooking them separately. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath. It's my perfect version of the holiday side—I tested it again and again, so it was worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

What People Are Saying:"[It's] an excellent recipe you can tweak it for taste. I like to up the onion by half again and use a lot more fresh sage." - GreenClover

"Using a [mandoline] made the final preparation fast and easy. It was a big hit over a lovely meal. The dressing brought high praise from two trained chefs." - RedFish

As I mentioned above, sourdough bread is my go-to for stuffing. The first step is to bake it! You'll need 2 sheets, or do this in batches. You want to dry it out, so bake for 15 to 20 minutes.

While that's toasting, it's time to cook the aromatics. Melt some butter, then cook the onions, leeks, and garlic until your kitchen smells amazing and everything is softened.

Time for the liquids: Simply whisk eggs, broth, milk, and some fresh herbs in a large measuring cup. You can use a touch of red pepper for a hint of spice, which I highly recommend, but if you have a spice-averse crowd, you can skip it.

When the bread is done toasting, turn the oven temp up to 375°. Prepare a 13" x 9" baking dish by coating it with a thin layer of butter.

Time to combine it all together: In a large bowl, mix the bread, aromatics, and liquid ingredients and toss until combined. You can let this sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour if you're planning ahead. Dot with even more butter, then bake until crispy. You can serve this stuffing warm or at room temperature.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

#6714. Where to Stay in Antwerp, Belgium’s Design-Filled City

Antwerp isn’t a loud city. You don’t come here to be awed by ancient ruins or to tour record-breaking skyscrapers. There are no leafy stoops with picturesque brownstones enshrined on TV. Antwerp’s charm unfolds quietly alongside its cobblestoned streets and narrow brick townhouses; I’d argue it’s a place most stumble upon when traveling through Europe, rather than specifically seek out. Those who do make it a point to visit, however, will easily be won over by its unassuming beauty and artistic milieu—after all, there’s a reason why it’s long attracted a certain kind of creative. (Painter Peter Paul Rubens called it home in the 16th century, fashion designers Raf Simons and Pieter Mulier do so in the 21st.)

Winter is an especially lovely time to visit—even when it drizzles (trust me, it will), Antwerp feels delightfully festive: Christmas markets take over the Old Town square, with glowing lights strung up all over the city. The ongoing Antwerp Six exhibit at the MoMu makes a trip this holiday season particularly timely; the group’s first major retrospective closes on January 17, 2027.

The best places to stay in Antwerp offer a chance to adjust to the city’s quiet rhythm—whether that means finding calm in a former convent, or slowing down in one of the many well-appointed Airbnbs that dot the center. Like most major European towns, you can confidently skip the car rental; much, if not most, of Antwerp, can be comfortably discovered on foot and by bike.

An Augustinian convent transformed into a design lover’s dream, the work of famed Belgian architect Vincent Van Duysen makes for a serene refuge after a long journey. Modernist touches and an earthy color palette underscore the property’s monastic qualities, and the rooms are thoughtful but efficiently put together. (The artfully rumpled bed linens are one highlight; the exposed timber beams in the larger suites, another.)

Couples wishing to explore the grounds can unwind with a treatment in the spa—which includes an intimate swimming pond—then dine in the on-site restaurant. (If weather allows, try to book a table in the outdoor terrace.) While the hotel is located in one of Antwerp’s quieter neighborhoods, het Groen Kwartier, you’re still within walking distance from most of the action, including two local favorites: Bar Vert for a low-key lunch, and Funk (an essential personal bookmark) for breakfast pastries.

Photo: Courtesy of Antwerp Botanic Sanctuary

It doesn’t get more central than this. Antwerp’s Botanic Sanctuary, the sole five-star property in town, gets its name from its location: It’s a former monastery nestled besides the city’s Botanical Gardens. Rooms are awash in calming neutrals with multiple large suites available for families—some of which overlook the adjoining 15th-century chapel. Food-motivated travelers are spoilt for choice: Start with drinks at Henry’s Bar, then take your pick of one of three Michelin-starred restaurants for dinner. (Ed note: The property’s marquee wellness facilities are currently temporarily closed due to a recent fire.)

Hotels in European Old Towns aren’t exactly known for their modern charm—and yet, Hotel Julien is brimming with exactly that. Set across two former historic buildings, it precedes the opening of its sister property August, but remains a worthwhile destination for its location alone. Rooms are cozy but pared back, punctuated by touches of red, and you’ll appreciate all the sightseeing there is to do, starting with the rooftop terrace that overlooks the Cathedral of Our Lady—an exalted edifice of Gothic architecture. It’s the ideal cozy home base for a trip spent exploring: “Antwerp is a very historic city, so it’s worth spending a day wandering through its streets, admiring the old architecture, and stepping into the many independent boutiques and antique shops,” adds de Geyter.

Originally a mansion built in 1890, Boulevard Leopold has found new life as a bed and breakfast since 2006. It’s very much no-frills—the aforementioned breakfast, a daily spread that includes croissants and fresh orange juice and is served each morning in the orangerie, is pretty much the only standard “amenity”—but that doesn’t mean it’s sparse. On the contrary, this jewel box of a space is full of charming little touches everywhere you look, the effect of which is a collected feel akin to that of a slightly eccentric aunt’s home.

To wit: crystal chandeliers that play against antler mounts, taxidermy birds that mingle with ornate, gilded candlesticks, a large bamboo fan moonlighting as a headboard that sits above a spartan cot. There are just five bedrooms to book, one of which is a gold-painted suite that takes up the entirety of the first floor. If you’re looking for a quiet, design-forward spot, this B&B is it.

Art is the main motivator at Hotel Pilar, a stylish boutique stay in Antwerp’s hip Het Zuid area, where each of its 21 rooms is designed around unique works. Oil paintings and glossy photographs contrast exposed brick and raw concrete in some; colorful prints juxtapose stainless steel and marbled tiles in others. Lively cafés and bars surround the property, which also happens to overlook the Royal Museum of Fine Arts (KMSKA). For the intrepid gallery hopper, the Museum of Contemporary Art (M HKA) is similarly close by; so is the Ann Demeulemeester flagship if you’re down for a side quest. An art-filled salon adjoins the hotel’s ground-floor restaurant—you’ll want to bookend the day here on one of its velvet couches, no matter where you dined that night.

Set in a 19th-century building in the heart of Antwerp’s fashion district, this light-filled apartment is a more than comfortable base from which to explore the city. It sleeps up to four, with a large dining room and sweet little kitchen that encourages culinary creativity. Original features, like a marble fireplace and antique wood floors, mix seamlessly with modern amenities; you will feel instantly at home.

Stained glass windows, zellige tiling, gilded mirrors… there are more than enough special decorative touches in this home to keep the eye busy. This stay is ideal for a family: It sleeps 10, with five distinctly designed bedrooms (the flamingo pink one, complete with a crystal chandelier and brocade drapes, feels especially grand). It’s well-located, too, with a green park nearby and several main tramlines on your cobblestoned doorstep.

#6712. The OG 'Thomas Crown Affair' Is an Essential Menswear Movie. How Will the Reboot Stack Up?

Between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the best of them is The Thomas Crown Affair, a 1968 caper film directed by Norman Jewison and starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Fast-forward a few days and the same could be said about the 1999 remake starring Bond-era Pierce Brosnan, which is worth watching for the suits alone.

Now, in other news of a formerly Brosnan-led, menswear-centric franchise being rebooted: Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan is the producer, director, and star of a third riff on The Thomas Crown Affair, as he announced at CinemaCon back in April. Judging by the first trailer that dropped last week, the film aims to uphold the sartorial reputation of its forebears.

Hitting theaters in March 2027, Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair remake follows the same premise as the 1968 and 1999 versions: a wealthy playboy businessman plots art heists for fun while being pursued by a sexy insurance investigator, played in this iteration by potential future Wonder Woman Adria Arjona. There’s crime, there’s glamour, there’s sexual tension—but most of all, in the spirit of the Thomas Crowns before him, there appears to be plenty of high-octane menswear. The movie’s style credit is bolstered by Ruth E. Carter, the two-time Oscar-winning costume designer of the Black Panther movies, who also dressed Jordan for his Oscar-winning turn in Sinners.

But how will MBJ’s high-fashion Thomas Crown land? In the trailer, he can be seen wearing a stiff gray shirt with a matching tie and trousers by Bottega Veneta. The shirt, marked by the luxury brand’s signature triangle pocket detail, had an odd fit: taut around the torso yet puffy around the biceps. Here’s hoping we’ll see some sharper tailoring in the next preview.

Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of big-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in The Thomas Crown Affair (1968).

Off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often said that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

Set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

#6710. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#6709. The Rise of the Maximum Visibility Bra

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The summer of 2014, I was a college student working at a small-town lingerie store that lined its walls exclusively with neutrals. Every day, I sold women flesh-toned bras—black if they were really feeling kinky—all while filling my own intimates drawer with the same styles. Undressing in front of a guy that same summer, he voiced genuine disbelief over my nude, industrial-strength strapless bra. He wasn’t so much confused over its gravity-defying function as the fact that it was there, at all.

The early 2010s set a nearly impossible goal for young women: naturally perky breasts without any apparent scaffolding. But that’s all changing. Pop princess Adela’s exposed bras have become as central to her identity as her electric pink hair. Once left to jiggle freely beneath semisheer cotton, Charli XCX’s chest is now more often displayed in intricate lingerie. Several months back, Saint Laurent’s Spring 2027 front row was littered with boudoir-inspired looks while Prada and Fendi literally sent bras-as-tops down the runway. Bras have come out of hiding.

Somewhere between the “free the nipple” movement in 2012 and the impending #MeToo revolution of 2017, boobs became less of a sexualized spectacle and more of a political battleground. Victoria’s Secret canceled its fashion show as basics-driven intimates brands like Cuup and Arq gained traction for destigmatizing natural shapes. Then, breasts bounced back into cultural focus. The shift might be credited to the climate—conservatism generally propels women to take shelter in traditional femininity, or it is thrust upon them—as well as the twin forces of Sydney Sweeney and semaglutide weight loss. Either way, women got thinner while their chests grew larger—reflecting a beauty standard we hadn’t seen in a generation. Implants entered a new era of demand and dialogue, as celebrities like Kylie Jenner and Megan Fox transparently joined the big-breasted brigade.

But boobs aren’t just bigger—they’re bolder. Gone are the days of basics and bralettes. It’s all about va-va-voom underwire, satin, and lace—even push-ups have returned to the conversation. Still, “there’s a difference between showing your bra and showing off your bra,” discerns Tara Ocello, director of brand marketing at intimates brand Skarlett Blue.

Last month, the recently revived Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show broadcast Jenner strutting down the runway, her 445-cc-moderate-profile silicones outfitted in a record-breaking $50 million bra. Bella Hadid, Candice Swanepoel, and Adriana Lima showed off the iconic mall brand’s finest embroidered balconettes, lacy push-ups, and satin plunge bras. Angels aside, the reintroduction of these runway collections is also indicative of a shift in consumer product demand—a spokesperson for Victoria’s Secret claims there’s “strong interest” in fashion-forward details like lace, satin, logo hardware, and the brand’s statement shine straps. The Very Sexy Push-Up Bra remains the number one of the three mainline bras in its “Very Sexy” category. “Today’s customer wants a bra that performs beautifully and deserves to be seen,” says a Victoria’s Secret spokesperson. “It’s expanded how customers engage with [our bras] as both foundation pieces and intentional styling elements.”

The luxury London retailer Agent Provocateur has been positioning its designs as statement pieces since it launched in the mid-’90s—the last time exposed bras enjoyed prevalence. Creative director Sarah Shotton noticed the trend bubbling several years back on the Glastonbury grounds and immediately returned to the design studio. “We predicted this and designed [for it] about a year and a half in advance. I am constantly thinking, could it be worn as an outerwear bra?” she says. “I think if customers are going to invest in it, they want it to work harder than just in the bedroom. Lingerie as outerwear is just getting bigger and bigger.”

Category transcension is, of course, good for business. Victoria’s Secret reported sales up 10 percent in its second quarter, and Agent Provocateur has also seen revenue growth this year. Eager to capitalize on the movement, contemporary brands like Lioness are now engineering built-in underwear to imitate the effect of an exposed bra. This week, Charlize Theron wore a similar style by Tom Ford to the Governors Awards.

I have, undoubtedly, been influenced. This year, I have spent more money at Victoria’s Secret than cumulatively on lingerie in the past decade—acquiring my own Very Sexy Push-Up, and a turquoise polka-dot number. These are bras I’ve never gravitated toward, let alone purchased, because they seemed like impractical additions to my wardrobe. I’ve had to ask myself: Can you wear leopard-print under a white tee? What if the lace breaches my neckline?

Somewhere between Erin Brockovich and Blake Lively’s character in The Town, an exposed bra—particularly a colorful one—became a media shorthand for unsophistication, and more often than not, sexual availability. In simpler terms: tacky. Now, tacky is trending. Along with diamanté-encrusted snapbacks and sky-high peep-toes, straps in dynamic hues are stretched across the décolleté of It girls en masse. Printed cups are peeking out of the necklines. Some fashionistas are forgoing the shirt altogether. “There's a real cultural shift from polished perfection toward something more expressive, unpredictable, and a little undone,” claims Ocello. Or, perhaps a little more human.

This certainly isn’t a trend for everyone. According to Shotton, Agent Provocateur’s biggest sellers are corsets—a style that was once also considered strictly lingerie, but has since sashayed into the light. One wonders if their popularity is a gateway to full bra-baring, especially as GLP drugs become more readily available, and women more comfortable in their bodies. But with a Blue Wave washing in Woke 3.0, how long do boobs—and their bold accessories—have left? In all seriousness, might we look back on this moment with the same disdain we once reflected on early-aughts raunch culture? Only social media will tell. In the meantime, I plan for my collection to keep growing.

#6708. The 8 Best Hotels in Santa Fe for a Winter Escape

Whatever expectations you might have for Santa Fe, nothing really prepares you for the magnitude of its beauty. The blue sky is enormous—with impossibly fluffy clouds—stretching on and on until it melts into the distance. The surrounding Sangre de Cristo (“blood of Christ”) mountains are especially striking, named by the Spanish who were spellbound by the peaks that turned a vivid red during sunrise and sunset. There’s the traditional adobe architecture the Southwest is famous for, earth-toned and low-slung, and the piñon-juniper woodlands that add to the landscape’s dreamlike quality. It’s a magical place where chiles and pine nuts are on every menu, and the craft scene is so prolific the city was designated a UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art. For travelers who have their sights set on New Mexico’s capital city, the best hotels in Santa Fe celebrate its many riches.

The city’s high-elevation desert climate makes visiting throughout the year a distinct experience. In winter, Santa Fe puts on its party hat and transforms into a holiday snow globe with glowing farolitos and city streets perfumed with piñon pine drifting from kiva fireplaces. Whether you choose to position yourself downtown in proximity to galleries and restaurants, or on the outskirts with wild acreage as your backyard, a winter spent in Santa Fe is certain to be a memorable one.

As you plan your upcoming travels, let Vogue’s guide to Santa Fe’s best hotels, below, serve as motivation to spend the cozy season in the Southwest.

Originally settled over 150 years ago by Jean Baptiste Lamy (the first Archbishop of Santa Fe), this property is now home to a luxury retreat surrounded by 317 acres bordering the Santa Fe National Forest. Guest rooms occupy adobe-style structures, with interiors that lean into the southwestern aesthetic—think, kiva fireplaces, wood beam ceilings, and decor sourced from local artists. The resort’s Adventure Basecamp acts as a meeting point for the day’s excursions, which range from horseback riding and guided hikes to a dedicated Ski Santa Fe experience in the winter.

For travelers who prefer a hotel amidst all the action, Vogue’s Senior Fashion and Style Writer Christian Allaire suggests Rosewood Inn of the Anasazi. “If you’re looking to explore around downtown Santa Fe, there are few better locations than here,” he says. “Situated right on the plaza, it's just steps away from all the action—but you may not want to leave, given how cozy the hotel is! The rooms come with wooden beams and fireplaces, and the restaurant serves up classic New Mexican fare with a modern twist.”

Despite its central location, the property feels like its own world once you step through the hand-painted, carved-wood doors. The interiors pay tribute to ancestral textiles and works by local indigenous artists, and chef Cristian Pontiggia (a James Beard Award semifinalist) blends New Mexico ingredients with global influences.

Set on 57 acres in the Sangre de Cristo foothills, Four Seasons Resort Ranch Encantado is a destination for travelers who want to be completely surrounded by nature (yet still situate themselves a convenient 10 minutes from the downtown area). There are 65 casita-style rooms designed with traditional materials like stucco exteriors, wood beams, and kiva fireplaces—plus private outdoor spaces for taking in bird chirps and the afternoon breeze. Thanks to the surrounding wilderness, activities run the gamut, from jeep tours to snowshoeing. Once you’ve worked up an appetite, head to Terra for roasted poblano leek bisque and an Ember & Adobe reposado cocktail.

With its convenient Barrio de Analco location and jewel box interiors, it’s no surprise The Inn of the Five Graces has won several prestigious design and travel awards over the years. “Each room is a feast for the eyes,” Abbas says, “a tapestry of colorful textiles, mosaic tiles, and handcrafted antiques that combine Southwestern decor with East Indian and Tibetan influences.” (If you fall in love with the decor and want to bring home a souvenir, the owners are also behind the furniture store Seret & Sons, which houses their grand collection.) For travelers staying on the property this winter, don’t miss seasonal activities like holiday tea time, fireside cocoa, and a holiday makers market.

This is not your average motel. This adobe roadside motor court was originally built in 1936 and is now home to one of Santa Fe’s most compelling boutique hotels. El Rey Court sits along old Route 66 and offers 86 rooms on five acres of old-growth gardens. No two adobe rooms are identical, and amenities like a heated outdoor swimming pool, a tree-lined lawn, and al fresco fireplace offer plenty of opportunities to soak in the natural surroundings. Be sure to spend at least one of your evenings at Le Reina, their mezcal and tequila bar that serves up a mean margarita.

This legendary hotel on Santa Fe’s iconic plaza sits on land that has played host to an inn since the early 17th century. La Fonda’s current structure dates back to 1922, and is now a member of the Historic Hotels of America association. Original details like hand-carved beams, terracotta tile, and stained glass skylights set a thoroughly romantic tone, while guest rooms keep it cozy with hand-painted headboards and earth tone decor.

For a home-away-from-home kind of getaway, this welcoming bed and breakfast offers eight rooms tucked among lush gardens. El Farolito is close to the city’s best attractions—to name a few: the historic plaza, farmer’s market, and Georgia O’Keefe Museum—yet sits on a tranquil street away from the bustle. The inn features original artwork throughout, as well as handmade furnishings like wood-carved headboards. And be sure to set your alarm for breakfast: It’s served from 7:30 to 9:30 every morning and can be blissfully enjoyed on the patio next to a gurgling fountain.

Unlike local lodging that leans into Southwest design aesthetics, the ryokan-style accommodations at Ten Thousand Waves offer a distinctly Japanese perspective. The spa is surrounded by 20 acres of piñons and junipers, and guest rooms are situated within a historic ranch house. This retreat is best for wellness-focused travelers, as the private hot tub suites and shared soaking environments are just a few steps away from the rooms. (Don’t sleep on the myofascial facial or shiatsu massage, either.) For cuisine, Izanami is an upscale izakaya serving seasonal small plates meant to share.
