#6689. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

Let's just say the health department had a few notes.

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety issues. The company paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!)

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

Big Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

#6688. The Governors Awards Marked the Official Start of the 'You Can See Everything' Oscars Campaign

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

Start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governors Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (and the esteemed Irving Thalberg Award) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

Dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had big presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he showed up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

When I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and said “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

But most importantly: the Governors Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governors Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I said “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

Later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya said Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a new Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

Other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

As for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly said that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

#6686. Joaquin Phoenix Wasn’t Thinking About 'Her' When He Filmed This Intelligent Eyewear Campaign

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

“Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner says. “It could be any language.”

The idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across New England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”

In an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”

#6685. Taco Bell Is Expanding Its Cantina Menu With Six New Steak Creations

Your usual order could be getting some serious competition.

Taste-testing Taco Bell's new FLAMIN' HOT menu items should've bought my stomach at least a few days off. Instead, the chain has already given me another reason to start thinking about my next order.

Taco Bell is testing a new carne asada protein across six menu items, giving its Cantina lineup another round of additions. But of course, there's a catch. As of November 12, it's only available in Nashville, Tennessee, and the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. So if you're lucky enough to live in either market, congratulations. I'll just be over here drooling over the pictures.

The steak itself sounds pretty different from what Taco Bell currently serves. It gets a marinade with citrus and savory seasonings before being cooked sous vide, then seared and cut into small chunks. Taco Bell says it's going for a deeper, more grilled flavor, and rather than giving it one or two menu appearances, the chain has come up with six ways to try it.

The Cantina Carne Asada Chalupa Lime Bowl is probably the most loaded of the bunch, piling steak, rice, black beans, guacamole, pico de gallo, cheese, and purple cabbage slaw together with chile-lime seasoned Chalupa Chips. There's also a Cantina Carne Asada Burrito, which wraps the meat in a new Sonoran-style flour tortilla with lettuce, cabbage, cheese, pico, and Spicy Ranch Sauce before getting grilled.

If tacos are more your speed, there are three options. The Cantina Carne Asada Crispy Taco comes in a fried corn shell with cheese grilled onto the outside, while the Cantina Carne Asada Soft Taco uses that same new flour tortilla with cabbage slaw and Spicy Ranch. Then there's the smaller Cantina Carne Asada Street Chalupa, which has a fried shell lined with crispy cheese.

Rounding things out is the Cantina Carne Asada Rolled Quesadilla, stuffed with steak, a three-cheese blend, and Spicy Ranch before being grilled and sliced. All six items also come with an Avocado Verde Salsa packet.

The rollout follows Taco Bell's push to give its Cantina menu more attention, including the slow-roasted chicken that's already made its way into items like the Cantina Chicken Mexican Pizza. This latest test could eventually put carne asada on the permanent menu, although there's no word yet on whether it'll expand beyond those two markets.

#6679. David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

#6678. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6677. Nike Made an Air Jordan 1 for Guys Who Love Japanese Denim

Menswear guys love Japanese denim. Menswear guys also love sneakers. So why not make some kicks for the people who can tell you exactly which artisanal mill produced their selvedge? That seems to be the thinking behind the new Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko.’

Social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same company behind A Ma Maniére. Over the years, it’s worked with Nike on everything from milk-inspired Dunks to Air Pennys. The shop’s last proper Jordan collab was an extremely hairy Air Jordan 6 from 2019, but now the pair are back with something a little easier to wear.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

Social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette. The toebox is white, the overlays are red, and the Swoosh and collar are black. But rather than keeping everything box-fresh, Social Status has roughed up the leather so it arrives pre-scuffed, as though you’ve owned these shoes for years.

The big switch happens across the sidewalls. The usual white leather panels have been replaced with mismatched patches of indigo fabric covered in white sashiko-style stitching. Sashiko is a traditional Japanese embroidery technique used to reinforce, repair, and extend the life of clothing. It’s particularly associated with vintage workwear and denim, which is why these Jordans look like they’ve been mended using a very expensive pair of jeans.

There’s also an old-school nylon tongue, a slightly aged sole, and a custom shoebox wrapped in the same blue pattern.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

While you might normally expect this sort of big Jordan release to land on the High, it’s nice to see the Low silhouette get some love. Some dudes prefer it, after all—it’s less bulky around the ankle and works better under wider trousers. You still get all the bits that make an Air Jordan 1 instantly recognizable, only without half the collar.

The Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’ is set to drop on December 18 for $155 through Social Status, with a wider release via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists expected to arrive later on. Japanese denim guys, get your credit cards ready.

#6674. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6673. Joseph Zada of The Hunger Games Is Still Getting Used to Being a Movie Star

Joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark. And why shouldn’t he be?

His much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week. Zada and I spoke the morning of his New York City premiere, while he was being shuttled from one press obligation to the next, already go-go-go before actually hitting the red carpet Monday night in custom Louis Vuitton, punctuated with a pair of gold-toed cowboy boots from Pharrell’s first collection for the brand.

In the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy. When asked about the movie, the 21-year-old Australian demonstrates palpable care and excitement, even a bit of sadness that it’s over. “I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes,” Zada says. “And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.”

Since being cast, he’s barely had a second to stop and reflect on joining one of the biggest franchises in the world—and this comes right on the heels of East of Eden, too, in which Zada played another haunted young man. He laughs when I note the comparison: “I guess I just pride myself on my ability to show my vulnerability.”

Below, read our full conversation with the emerging star as he reflects on his Hunger Games journey, talks red carpet style, and shares his thoughts on Robert Pattinson playing James Bond.

Joseph Zada: Yeah, I wonder if I’ll be nervous.

Maybe towards the start. It doesn’t get old… but it gets familiar.

Well, I did SiriusXM this morning, and then, I mean, it’s basically just been like, "Hey, do press all day and then go to your premiere." So there’s not much time for a ritual, so I guess I go a little bit nonverbal and half-dissociate.

No, it’s so much fun. I have a lot of fun at these premieres. It’s always like a crazy, crazy crowd. The way they’ve set it up has just been otherworldly, and I’m not sure if I’ll ever have it again, but I distinctly remember each stop and the feelings that I’ve had thus far, and it doesn’t get old. It’s always crazy to see this many fans and the passion they have for this project. I mean, it’s not every day that you get to step into something with a built-in fan base where people are already coming out and supporting it before they’ve even seen it. So it’s a really special experience, and I don’t know when I’m going to be able to get that again.

Where did I have the most fun? I had a lot of fun in London because my little sister was there, my little sister and my brother’s girlfriend, so I got to hang out with them and I haven’t seen them in a while. And Mexico. Mexico was the craziest event that we’ve had. There were literally thousands, several thousands of people there. The reception was incredible.

Am I allowed to drop this? Oh, yes, that is what this [interview] is for. I’m wearing a Louis Vuitton suit—custom, custom—that Jason [Bolden] and I have worked together on, and I’m a big fan of the boots. The boots are pretty dope.

I feel a lot more comfortable in these clothes nowadays, and it’s actually become a lot more enjoyable to put them on. And it feels like more of an armor and less of a scary thing, and it feels like I build a lot of confidence being able to do this.

My red carpet style, I think... I don’t know. Just whatever Jason puts me in for the night.

Yeah, I think just doing it so often and finding different looks and just being able to wear all the different brands and find what I’m comfortable in.

I pride myself on my ability to have vulnerability. I think as a young man, that’s what I find interesting in these performances of these young men coming of age, and I think that was really what I was just looking for in my early career. I modeled my career on people like Timothée Chalamet and Lucas Hedges, and I love the way that they kept their heart on their sleeve and how they feel like an open nerve. I love being able to portray that in my performances.

I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes and really, really felt like I was there every single day and just had the most incredible support in terms of my cast mates and my directors and my producers. And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.

I guess everything just kind of changed just like that. Everything just changed in one quick second, and it feels like... I guess I haven’t really thought about what it was like before. I’ve just kind of been trying to ride the wave. I’m sure being able to go back home for Christmas, I’ll have some time to reflect, but right now it’s just—what’s the day ahead of me? And just making sure I’m ready for all of that.

I’m just excited to be at home every single day and watch movies with my mom and my siblings and see all my friends. That’s what I’m really excited for. I’m just excited to also just turn off my phone for a little bit, maybe go on a little road trip down to South Australia and get a little beach house and not bring my phone and have six days where I’m just off the grid.

That’s a great question. I’ve got Apocalypse Now on 4K Ultra HD on my projector that I bought at home, and I cannot wait. I feel like people ask me what was the best part of my year, and I just start naming all the movies that I’ve watched. And genuinely the happiest that I ever am is when I’m watching a film, which is kind of sad but also kind of cool.

I think... I don’t know. I loved Wild Horse Nine. That’s a favorite I’ve watched in cinemas. I loved Primetime too, because I love Rob Pattinson. I love Skyler Gisondo.

I did just see the Bond casting news! I am chuffed. That is so exciting. That is beyond exciting. He is just the most phenomenal actor, and he really just makes the most interesting choices. And I think him in that role, the stoicism that he’ll bring along with those really interesting choices, it’s going to make that character so interesting. He’s a really special actor. It feels like every young male actor that I speak to feels like that is a person to look to right now and a person’s career to emulate in terms of the risks and the commitment to his craft and all these roles that he’s churning out.

I don’t know. It’s so ridiculously helpful to have a book with you because it’s just so much information, and I love preparing for roles and having a book because it’s just an internal monologue, which is what you should be doing for every character. You read a scene, and you should be writing what is going through your character’s head. And when you have a book, it’s all done for you, or at least you have a good foundation.

I hope I get to do as many book adaptations as possible, but I think what I’m really looking for is just a great director and a great script. I’m not sure what’s [next]. I’ve got a fresh slate right now, but there’s a couple of things floating around.

#6672. DoorDash Reveals The Thanksgiving Desserts & Sides Each State Loves

Somebody might want to check on the pumpkin pie loyalists.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

During a Thanksgiving food debate, everyone at the table likely has a strong opinion. DoorDash just added some numbers to the argument, and they might surprise you—especially if you assumed pumpkin pie was untouchable.

Ahead of Thanksgiving 2026, the delivery company went ahead and analyzed what Americans ordered during last year's holiday, and apparently, we've got some explaining to do. From an unexpected dessert taking the national crown to some questionable side-dish allegiances, the results make a pretty convincing case that no two Thanksgiving tables are exactly alike.

According to DoorDash's 2025 ordering data, chocolate cake was the most popular store-bought pie or cake purchased through the platform during Thanksgiving week. Apple pie came in second, followed by cheesecake. Pumpkin pie, arguably the holiday's most recognizable dessert, had to settle for fourth place, with pound cake rounding out the top five.

Things get even more interesting when you look at individual states. DoorDash also identified which desserts each state ordered at a higher rate than the national average, revealing some pretty distinct regional preferences.

Pumpkin pie still had plenty of supporters, with strong support in 14 states, including California, Washington, and Arizona. Hawaii was especially devoted, ordering it at nearly three times the national share. Meanwhile, New York, Connecticut, and Massachusetts leaned toward apple pie, while New Jersey and Pennsylvania showed a particular fondness for pound cake.

Cheesecake stood out in eight states, including Illinois, Michigan, and Ohio. Texas, Louisiana, and Tennessee favored pecan pie, while Maine and New Hampshire were among the states where chocolate pie stood out.

And then there's Georgia, where key lime pie was the surprising choice.

Mashed potatoes topped DoorDash's national Thanksgiving-week ranking, followed by corn, sweet potatoes, green beans, and gravy. Mac and cheese, stuffing, cornbread, carrots, and cranberries also made the top 10.

Regionally, though, things get a little more interesting. Cornbread stood out in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, while North Carolina and South Carolina showed a preference for mac and cheese. Tennessee's standout was biscuits, and Georgia, Alabama, and Florida leaned toward corn.

New York and New Jersey, two states that can barely agree on pizza, apparently found some common ground in carrots. Meanwhile, Vermont was the only state where stuffing stood out most, and neighboring New Hampshire went with squash.

It's worth remembering that these state rankings reflect what people ordered more frequently relative to the national average on DoorDash. They aren't necessarily each state's most popular dish overall, and they don't account for whatever Grandma was making from scratch.

Still, if someone tries to tell you there's only one acceptable Thanksgiving menu, you now have some pretty compelling evidence to the contrary.

#6670. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6669. Robert Pattinson, I’m Begging You For a Quirked-Up James Bond

Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007. Finally we can stop the debates and fan-casting and let Patts and Denis Villeneuve cook until they’re ready to present their new vision. But that would require a level of restraint that the internet doesn’t typically exercise. Immediately after the protracted process of casting Bond concluded, the internet moved on to naming its dream picks for Bond Girls and Bond Villains (sometimes, to brilliant effect.) I can’t say I have a dog in either fight, at least not right now. My Bond WishList is of a different magnitude altogether: can we make James Bond silly again? Just a little, even, 15 percent goofball?

In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve. But the best thing about Pattinson is his range. Sure, if Villeneuve and co. want to render Bond as the stoic and taciturn gentleman he’s generally been this century, Rob has proven he can do that, as every Tenet truther has been gleefully preaching for the last 24 hours. But more often than not, Pattinson is keen to get weird, whether that’s going Full Freak, as he does in Primetime, or approaching certain archetypal parts with a silly, goofy mood (like his conniving suitor in The Odyssey). He can do a “voice” (Mickey 17), he can do scumbag grime (Good Time), he can do hapless screwball (The Drama). Why not make what’ll be his biggest role to date a little cocktail of all his best elements? (Okay, he can leave the Mickey 17 voice behind.)

20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era. But in the past two decades, the pendulum has swung back—the gritty reboot has become studios' stock-in-trade. I feel the same way about Batman; the actual risky choice would be to make something less like Nolan’s series that, instead, hewed a little closer to, say, Batman Forever, or even the gothic camp of Tim Burton’s two films.

Of course, Robert Pattinson was at the center of a Batman reboot as well, and the result was a movie that felt more like a spiritual cousin to David Fincher’s Se7en; audiences ate it up so much that the hunger for a sequel persists even after endless delays. When it comes to franchises as high-stakes as Batman or Bond, you can’t trust these increasingly sauceless execs to make anything but the basic choice. There’s no reason to expect Jeff Bezos isn’t texting Denis screenshots from Skyfall for reference from his megayacht at this very moment.

But if there’s anybody capable of putting a little English on the handle while still giving the mainstream what it wants, it’s Big Bob Pattinson. He could easily make his James Bond a little off, or he could go full seductive cad who smiles like Neil Tenet, has a ki with Q, and charms women with some playful banter instead of simply brooding them into submission. I’m not looking for invisible cars and sharks with lasers, or a Lothario like Roger Moore who speaks in puns. All I’m asking is that we give camp a chance. Because ultimately, the most exciting thing Villeneuve and Pattinson can do to set their Bond apart would be to loosen him up a little.

#6668. Patrick Schwarzenegger Says This Small Detail Makes All The Difference In A Great Martini (Exclusive)

Three years with one of vodka's oldest families will apparently teach you a few things.

Patrick Schwarzenegger knows a thing or two about a good martini. After three years working with Ketel One and spending time with the family behind the vodka, the White Lotus actor has learned that some people take their cocktails very seriously.

"I'm not that severe," Schwarzenegger told me, although he's developed a few preferences of his own. His biggest? "A frosted glass. A cold glass I think makes all the difference."

I caught up with Schwarzenegger in Schiedam, Netherlands, during a Ketel One-hosted visit to the historic Nolet Distillery, where the family has been making spirits since 1691. The trip was actually his idea. After hearing so much about the distillery from the Nolet family, Schwarzenegger wanted to see everything firsthand, even getting his hands dirty by shoveling coal into the distilling equipment.

According to Schwarzenegger, family members have gotten so particular about their drinks that they'll check where a bar stores its vermouth, olives, and white wine before ordering. If certain ingredients have been sitting out rather than refrigerated, they might opt for a drier martini.

Bob Nolet sees that same attention to detail in the way people order cocktails today. "Today's martini drinkers know what they want," he told Delish, whether that's a classic dry martini, something dirty, or an espresso version.

Of course, that hasn't stopped bartenders from seeing just how far they can stretch the definition of a martini. Schwarzenegger told me he tried The Corner Store’s viral sour cream-and-onion version largely because he'd heard so much about it, something he deemed “really good.”

The Tomatini was another story. He appreciated how convincingly it captured tomato flavor, but the novelty only went so far. "I think that I could have that for a few sips, maybe one max, but then I'm tapped out of that," he said.

His more dependable order is an espresso martini, something the Nolets know particularly well. Schwarzenegger revealed that the family even arranged for espresso machines to be sent to his wedding in Idaho, giving guests a way to enjoy his favorite cocktail during the celebration.

For Carl Nolet Jr., the connection goes deeper than a shared appreciation for espresso martinis. "Patrick comes from a family that is equally committed to their craft in the entertainment space," he told Delish. "You can see that commitment through his career and how he brings his legacy into a new generation."

Carl also credits Schwarzenegger with offering a younger perspective on cocktail culture, particularly how drinking has become part of the way people socialize, host, and celebrate.

For someone who knows his way around a cocktail, Schwarzenegger doesn't actually drink all that often. Between filming, fitness, and work, he's made a rule to keep alcohol to weekends. He's also taken an interest in the growing demand for better-for-you options, pointing to canned cocktails with less sugar and real fruit juice as examples of how people's drinking habits are changing.

That curiosity extends well beyond the bar. With his involvement in the protein snack company MOSH, Schwarzenegger has become the kind of person who considers wandering supermarket aisles a perfectly good Friday night activity. One of his first stops after arriving in the Netherlands was a grocery store, and he loves comparing what's available in different places, from Los Angeles to wife Abby Champion's home state of Alabama.

His Instagram algorithm isn't helping matters, either. Food, drinks, random syrups—if an ad catches his attention, there's a decent chance it'll end up on his doorstep. "I buy everything," he admitted.

Interestingly, all that enthusiasm for trying new things doesn't necessarily translate to elaborate dinners. He and Champion love exploring restaurants together, but they're equally happy cooking at home or keeping things simple. She's a fan of Chick-fil-A and In-N-Out, while he's perfectly content with a plate of chicken and rice.

After talking martinis with Schwarzenegger and the Nolets, I might start paying a little more attention to what happens behind the bar. I'll leave the vermouth inspections to the professionals, but keeping the rest of my martini on ice until I'm ready for a fresh, frosty glass? That's a level of service I could get used to.

#6666. Upgrade Your Basics: Best Undershirts for Men in 2026

Just because you don't see a building's foundation doesn't mean it isn't holding everything up. In much the same way, the best undershirts for men are the humble base layer of countless great outfits. Many GQ staffers, in fact, wear-test theirs daily, and yet they're often overlooked, even though they've long-perfected their role: to be the protective layer between your gross body and your steezy, attention-hungry shirts and polos.

And while they're certainly good for some added warmth in the winter, there's a common misconception that they can make the wearer too hot. In fact, lightweight, moisture-wicking undershirts made from fabrics like modal, or cotton blends can actually transfer the sweat away from your body, speeding up your cooling down. All that's to say: Undershirts are more than just men’s underwear. They’re the cornerstone of a hall-of-fame fit.

An undershirt is an undershirt is an undershirt. If you want the most straightforward version, the kind that you’re picturing in your head is most likely from Calvin Klein. It’s a classic crewneck undershirt that’s made of a lightweight jersey that’s 100% cotton which has a smooth, very slightly brushed hand that feels worn-in in the best way possible. The slim fit won’t cause any weird bunching or bulging and it’s got enough length to stay tucked even when you’re out on the town cutting rugs.

My colleague, GQ senior commerce editor Avidan Grossman, has been wearing CK's genre-defining undershirts since his high school years. (He could do without the logo at the hem, but has made his peace with it, given that you never see it once it's tucked.) Otherwise, he prizes Calvin Klein's riff for its simple, pared-down design and blessed lack of modern-day frills. After all, not every shirt needs to moisture wick or odor block. If you just want an undershirt that gets the job done, don't overthink it.

Sometimes, sleeves are just too much undershirt. That’s where tanks come in. Also known as A-shirts, the humble, sleeveless tank has been rocked by every heartthrob and neighborhood grandpa as far back as anyone can remember. And while the low neck and lack of sleeves means you’ll practically never see them underneath a button-up, the irony is that they look great shown off with an unbuttoned camp shirt or on their own.

For the money, we think Hanes takes the cake with their multipack of undershirts. The stretchy ribbed jersey is made of 100% cotton and fits snug with a low neck that’s slightly squared off compared to most tanks. They may cost just under twenty bucks for a pack of six, but they look like a million bucks. “I’ve had buyer's remorse over many a menswear garment over the years,” explains GQ editor Jordan Bowman, "but the one thing that has never let me down is the humble tank top from Hanes. They nailed the fit and the material, and the great thing is, you can buy a pack just about anywhere."

If every part of your wardrobe has to be fit for a king, down to the most basics of basics, then CDLP is what we’d recommend, my liege. The reality is that most luxury tees don’t offer much more than the regular stuff. It’s diminishing returns after a certain price point, but CDLP is the notable exception. My colleague, our contributing editor Louis Cheslaw, has put his same CDLP cottons through the ringer year after year, and says they still haven't lost their luster.

It’s a pricey undershirt, for sure, but the high-quality fabric has a silky hand and lightweight feel that’s unparalleled. (It really feels like you’re almost wearing nothing.) Thanks to a wider neckline, you’re a lot less likely to see the tee poking out, too. And if you feel like such a nice T-shirt is wasted as underwear, don’t worry—the cut and shorter length means it looks great untucked, and can double as your regular T-shirt too.

Mack Weldon’s silver series of garments is what happens when you get nerdy about chemistry and fashion (in the best possible way). The Ionic+ technology embeds silver charged silver ions which are naturally antimicrobial into the fabric itself. Essentially, that means bacteria and odor is neutralized, which means you can take it easy on the deodorant. Beyond that, the tees are made of super long staple Supima cotton and a smidge of lycra for an extra silky fee, comfortable stretch, and long-lasting wear.

The main bummer is that they’ll cost you more than most tees, so stocking up for the week can get pricey. Still, it’s one of those undershirts that makes you realize you’ve been settling for squalor—plus, you can bundle up and get 10% off to help offset the sticker shock.

Not everything at Uniqlo is a great value. But when it comes to upgraded basics at an affordable price, you’d be hard-pressed to find brand that does it better. When you need an airy, breathable undershirt that's truly lightweight, the Japanese mega-retailer’s AIRism tees are legendary. They’re crafted from a smooth and breathable cotton-polyester-spandex blend that dries quickly, feels cool to the touch, and fights odors—a triple threat that’ll have sweaty days in a headlock. I personally wear these—they're a failsafe way to save my expensive dress shirts from dreaded pit stains, but they’re also perfect for wearing as a gym shirt. And at just $15 per tee, there’s no other undershirt that can do as much for the price.

GQ contributor Evan Malachosky was always a little skeptical of Skims, but the brand's tees won him over. He found that Skims’s proprietary fabrics are silky on the skin, and are neither too thin (and therefore exposing), nor too thick (and therefore too hot). Pleasingly, the brand has applied just as much care to its undershirt, even though—or perhaps because—it's designed to look invisible under your clothes. (The design team even thought about cleaning up the seam lines, so nothing would show through.) Made from 100% cotton, and available in an incredibly wide range of sizes, our favorite detail is that it's a little bit longer than the brand's standard tees, so that there's no risk of any unsightly seams being visible at the hemline, either.

If the purpose of an undershirt is to fly under the radar, then it stands to reason that a V-neck one—which remains invisible even when you unbutton your shirt collar—might be the most efficient of all the styles here. You'll still want to trust the classic makers here, which is why our favorite comes from Calvin Klein. Like the Calvin Klein crewneck option above, the fabric is smooth, slightly brushed, and 100% cotton. It's also affordable, and available in not just white, black, and gray, but also a multipack comprising all three. Lastly, CK's trademark slimmer fit means no bunching or bulging risk.

Are these “undershirts” far heavier than the usual ones? Yes. But they never lose their shape, and if you live in a bitterly cold climate, you'll want even your undershirt to max out its warming properties.

The luxury car of undershirts, Falke's premium undershirts go on just as smoothly (and last just as long) as the beloved German brand's famous socks.

You heard it here first: Ralph Lauren's Pony has become the coolest label in menswear again.

When James Bond—well, Daniel Craig as James Bond—needs an undershirt, he wears Sunspel's.

Kirkland Signature is somewhat of a fashion industry secret. These are made of soft, long-staple Egyptian cotton, and they're tube knit, meaning you don't have to worry about any uncomfortable side seams.

Made from rayon and polyester, Hanes’ moisture-wicking undershirts are fast-drying, cool to the touch, and silky smooth, all for just $5 a pop.

If you wanna let your clavicles shine uninhibited by any undershirt peek-age, a V-neck is the best way (short of a tank) to do it.

Cut from a premium cotton, this lightweight undershirt is going to feel a little thicker and warmer than others on this list, purely because Reigning Champ's premium cotton fabrics tend to lean towards the beefier end of the spectrum.

Though Mack Weldon’s 18-Hour Rib Tank doesn’t come with the microbe-smashing odor technology as their Silver crew neck undershirt, it does have an even silkier fabric and plenty of stretch.

The first thing I noticed when I met Wythe's founder was not his jeans, or amazing western shirt. It was actually this ribbed tank.

Undershirts are meant to be that intermediate layer between your outermost layers and your body, a protective guard that keeps your star garments fresh and free of sweat. Therefore, it's materials, construction, and fit that are the main components that determine how good an undershirt (and, well, every garment) actually is.

Above all else, your undershirt's fabric should be breathable, soft, comfortable, and, ideally, sweat-wicking. We primarily love undershirts and tanks that are made from high-quality 100% cotton, which has many of those characteristics naturally, but we also feel like there’s a time and place for synthetics, which are often used for their ability to wick away moisture and dry easily—especially for those who run particularly hot. And note: Stretchy materials like Spandex are helpful for comfort, but their elasticity will eventually degrade over time.

Undershirts should almost always fit closer to the body than your regular T-shirts. This is because they’ll be layered underneath another shirt or sweater, and can bunch in odd ways if too baggy. They don’t need to be skin-tight, but they should be slim enough to layer comfortably and long enough to tuck into your shirt. In fact, Peter Middleton, founder of Wythe, even told us that they should fit slim to start, since they are cotton and are knit, and will therefore stretch a little over time. If they are loose to start with, they are only going to become looser and saggier, which is really not the point.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

It’s the most wonderful (and caffeinated) time of the year.

Starbucks has already unveiled its 2026 holiday cup designs, including an adorable miniature version for dogs. Now it's time for the humans to get their hands on something they can actually keep.

But before you make a special trip for a little piece of festive plastic, a few things are worth knowing, as your usual coffee order might need some adjusting.

Circle Tuesday, November 17, on your calendar, as that's when Starbucks will be handing out its latest reusable holiday cups at participating locations across the country.

The catch is that it’s only happening while supplies last. And considering how much people love free stuff, I wouldn't recommend waiting until a 4 p.m. coffee run to try your hand at getting a cup.

Starbucks says it's bringing in extra baristas for the occasion, too, which should help with the inevitable rush of customers looking to add to their collections.

You'll need to purchase a qualifying handcrafted holiday or fall beverage of any size. Yes, even a tall gets you the same free 16-ounce cup as someone ordering a venti.

You don't even have to physically step inside a Starbucks, either. Orders placed at the drive-thru, through the app, or via DoorDash, Grubhub, and Uber Eats are all eligible.

And somehow, brewed Starbucks Christmas Blend and Starbucks Reserve Christmas coffee don't qualify, despite having Christmas right there in their names. Because apparently, even Christmas itself can't get you a free cup.

This year's version features coffee cherries and leafy branches tied together with a big red bow. There's also a green-and-white ribbon design around the outside that ties into the rest of Starbucks' holiday collection.

The reusable cup is made with 95 percent recycled material, and unlike the paper versions you normally toss after finishing your latte, this one is meant to stick around.

In fact, putting it back to work comes with a few perks. Bring a clean reusable cup to Starbucks on a future visit, and you'll save 10 cents on your drink, while Rewards members also get double Stars on their entire order.

#6663. Grand Theft Auto VI Review: Better Than The Hype

There are moments in GTA 6 that’ll have you levitating off your sofa. Unprecedented in its scope and production, it was created by a team of almost 5,000 developers over nearly 10 years. Its budget is rumored to rival the construction of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper; its first trailer set records with 93 million views in a day. Every social media brand account, from the White House to BMW, has jumped on the hype, while economists predict a national sick day as millions play hooky to game. When you do, you see the time, talent and flair on the screen. But, at its heart, Grand Theft Auto VI follows in series tradition: an epic American crime story, set in a stunning parody of the US that riffs on film, music, politics, style and satire.

Fronting the first franchise entry in more than 13 years are Jason and Lucia. Developer Rockstar attempted a multi-character arc in Grand Theft Auto V, but those three leads learned to loathe one another. Instead, VI tackles love, a game design challenge most developers have sworn off with good reason. Not a parent/child relationship like The Last of Us or God of War, but a mature, romantic, adult one. You can call or text each other at pretty much any point—to do missions together, commit robberies, explore, meditate, work out, fly, or just to coexist under the Vice City sunshine.

This isn’t some kind of ChatGPT fantasy to indulge in. Neither Jason or Lucia exists at your beck and call as some kind of hyper-realistic plaything. You have a role in their relationship, both in the way they speak to each other and where the story takes them. You can cruise down the Vice City waterfront together in your souped-up ’70s muscle wagon with one of you driving, the other scrolling through your Snapmatic feed (the in-game social media channel), before grabbing a drink and carving up the sidewalk with an assault rifle five minutes later. You just don’t get these detours in Call of Duty.

More than a car: in GTA VI, your vehicle is a mobile base of operations to stash your guns, fits, money, and drugs.

It’s a different pace from previous Grand Theft Autos too. Rockstar changed its dynamics with 2018’s Red Dead Redemption 2—a more thoughtful take on the outlaw tale that added friction to the action and a conscience to the narrative. For a developer that once experienced the spotlight of US Congress during 2005’s infamous “Hot Coffee" controversy (when a sexually explicit mini-game meant as an inside joke between developers was figured out by savvy users), this kind of nuance was revelatory. With VI, Rockstar takes Red Dead 2’s ethos and applies it to a modern city with 1,000 x the population. The result is staggering, but still an absolute blast to play. That is to say, the greatest hits of GTA—driving cars, shooting guns, and stealing money, drugs and more (all to spend on a better Beretta, G-Wagon replica, and impeccably modeled Air Jordan dupes)—but with added depth to how you play. Weapon slots are finite; you can no longer run amok with an entire arsenal stashed in your jacket pocket. Money is vulnerable; get killed or caught with cash in your possession, and you’ll lose it. And if you jack a car that’s fitted with a tracker, the police will find you quickly.

Should you get into a bust-up with the law after a jewelry store smash-and-grab gone wrong, the game’s action is frenetic. Roads are much narrower, traffic is denser, and you can’t see police on your minimap. That $40,000 in cash sitting on the back seat had better be worth the hassle. As such, the game supports your decision to play chaotically, but truly immerses you in playing methodically. Jason and Lucia each have a “criminal profile”—be unnecessarily violent and you’ll get a “psycho” rating—that adds replayability and roleplay. Still, I had the most fun when planning missions: using a silenced pistol, shooting to maim not kill, and wiping security footage to leave no trace. It’s the closest GTA has honed in on the art of crime. The feds will surround the store you’re robbing. “Come out right now with your hands above your head!” Do things right, and you’ll have prepped your partner with a getaway car out back. You’ll leave the scene anonymously as backup blares past you on the other side of the road.

Every club, pub and dingy dive bar in GTA 6’s Leonida has a distinct vibe—from the music to the decor to the sweaty Floridians inside.

The game kicks off with an electrifying setup accompanied by an original song from composers Justice. It perfectly sets the tone: VI has the ’80s flamboyance of Vice City made new and fresh. It takes its opening hours steadily, sending you on odd jobs to make a little money here and there. Gradually—then suddenly—you’re thrust into the most high-octane campaign in Grand Theft Auto history. Tense hospital escapes, daring bank heists, cross-country chases, and more. Its set pieces are balls-to-the-wall bravado, rivaling what you’d see in Nolan’s The Odyssey or Villeneuve’s Dune, upping in intensity through its chapters. Tonally, it’s the most “of the now” Grand Theft Auto game yet, as your two in-love criminals race to find a better life in an unfair world. No previous GTA has given you a savings account—it’s like playing the millennial curse. The only dings are some pacing in the game’s second chapter as the game wrestles with its story while still introducing mechanics. Think of it as VI’s version of RDR2’s Guarma, albeit with bargain bin stores and grimy strip malls instead of exotic Caribbean fauna.

And then to Leonida, with which Rockstar has created the most technically and artistically impressive game world ever made. The pre-release trailers promised beaches bustling with vacationers and nightclubs packed with dancers. That is the reality. From sea to sand to sky, the world is alive. Vice City alone could be an entire game in its own right, complete with distinct districts, an explorable international airport, and more. Yet, Rockstar spoils us with a massive expanse of varied towns, high-class beach resorts, lush green national parks, murky swamplands and sun-kissed island keys. All packed with people that range from useful, to funny, to completely unsavory (shout-out to the old woman who took one look at my Jason and said “I’mma take my teeth out and suck the skin off that dick”). The density and fidelity of it all often stretches the limits of even Sony’s PlayStation 5 Pro. Frame rate dips don’t spoil gameplay, but the slowdown is noticeable when you’ve punted a couple of grenades into passing cars to set off multiple explosions at once.

NPCs don’t just feel like backdrop mannequins anymore, but real people with an incredible range of faces, body types and outfits.

Every frame a photograph. Stop anywhere in GTA 6, and you’ll likely find something enticing to see, hear or interact with.

As with Red Dead Redemption 2, the most impressive of the game’s many achievements is how everything seems to live on without you. All it took to make this world was Rockstar founding an entire studio to work solely on Leonida’s population. I’ve seen a woman throw herself out of a cop car window as I scooted along Ocean Beach, and car thieves burst through the glass windows of a car dealership while the alarms howl. I saw a furry taken down by armed police, staged perfectly with a helicopter spotlight. During one 3 a.m. wander through the rough neighborhood of Crosstown, a man approached me to warn me of the local gang and tells me they have a nearby base. I accidentally tapped the button that brings up your in-game phone. “Ohhhh! You don’t just believe what I say” the man says, responding to my actions. “You do your own research!” In more than 70 hours of play, I have seen only one moment of repetition.

There is so much more besides. A cast of interesting, funny and believable characters; off-the-beaten-path secrets that can lead to side quests both big and small; perhaps the best radio track list of any GTA spanning from Travis Scott to Lana Del Rey; podcast episodes; golf to play; gators to hunt; dozens of supercars to steal and customize; weapons that feel punchy and satisfying; multiple racing series; a litany of actually interesting shops and bars and clubs to explore and buy things in. I’ve seen brilliant horror vignettes, startling science fiction, and laugh-out-loud comedy just by exploring. Rockstar has created a world that rewards you for spending time in it. Expect to spend 100 hours if you want to see everything.

As you’ll likely have seen and heard—in everything from Miami Heat takeovers, to Netflix launches, to Selfridges pop-ups—that this is the most-wanted entertainment property in the world. In a way, all it had to be was Grand Theft Auto V: The Second. But, on the largest and most scrutinized stage imaginable, Rockstar takes creative risks with its story, protagonists, and mechanics, and makes big leaps in what games can be. It’s unlikely other developers will catch up soon. In 2002, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City reshaped and refashioned pop culture to give us a playable version of a place and a time we already knew. A quarter of a century later, VI shows Rockstar at the peak of entertainment in its very own right.

#6662. Kate Middleton Shopped From Brentwood to Belgravia for Her Royal Tour

Last night, the Prince and Princess of Wales took to the red carpet for this year’s Earthshot Prize Awards, the centerpiece of their three-day tour of Mumbai and New Delhi. The ceremony awarded five environmental projects—tackling everything from forever chemicals in France to the protection of marine life in the Pacific Islands—over $1 million each to further their work. Making her first appearance at the event since she travelled to Boston in 2022, Catherine wore a hand-embroidered anarkali by Mahima Mahajan, which she is believed to have purchased for a modest—at least by royal standards—$892 from Lilly’s Boutique in Essex. (Perhaps during her visit to The Forward Trust in nearby Southend-on-Sea back in September?)

But this morning, on the final day of their trip, the Kate Middleton we know was back on more rarefied ground, stepping out in a tailored, fit-and-flare dress of cherry-red wool crepe by Sloane Street-based designer Emilia Wickstead, priced at $2,461. From Brentwood to Belgravia, then; two very different sides of the British retail landscape, both represented in the same suitcase. Alongside her trusty suede Manolo Blahniks and coordinating DeMellier Small Hudson bag were the additions of a hand-embroidered shawl and beaded bracelet, presented to her during a visit to the Chanakya School of Craft in Mumbai, which trains women from underserved communities in traditional Indian techniques and has paired up its graduates with the likes of Dior, Fendi, and Valentino. The Princess then traveled to the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital, known for offering affordable care to women from all walks of life.

Whether Catherine has another outfit change in her suitcase—she and William are due to attend a bilateral meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi before returning to Windsor—remains to be seen. What this trip has made clear, though, is that the future Queen Kate Middleton is as intentional with her wardrobe as ever. Consider the rewears—sustainable choices, yes, but also ones that avoid headlines about new purchases that might distract from the work at hand—or the range of price points, from relatively accessible DeMellier handbags to priceless jewels from the royal collection. Above all, though, is her continued ambassadorship of British fashion—a concept as ever-changing and expansive as the country’s identity itself—as demonstrated by an Indian-designed dress bought on an English shopping street.

#6661. Upside-Down Apple Cider Cheesecake

If you feel there’s never enough graham cracker crust with your cheesecake, then this version is for you. The entire no-bake cheesecake is surrounded by crust, so there are buttery graham crackers and creamy cheesecake in every single bite. The exterior isn’t just hiding a silky-smooth cheesecake filling, but also a surprise syrupy apple filling. If you want to win the holidays this year, set this unassuming dessert on the table and watch everyone ooh and ahh as they cut in and discover the sweet, spiced, and completely delicious treat hiding inside.

How to make it upside-down:To achieve a double layer of crust, you need to freeze one layer so that it’s easy to place on top of the cheesecake. Before serving, you’ll flip the whole thing onto a plate, which puts the seam on the bottom and gives you a beautiful display of a solid crust. It’s easier than you think to flip it, and the parchment will ensure nothing sticks to the springform pan.

Make ahead & storage:I love to make this dessert during the holidays because you can prep and make it all ahead of time. The apple filling can be made up to 3 days ahead, and the assembled cheesecake can be made up to 2 days ahead of when you want to serve.
