#6638. Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, New York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

As soon as the volunteer says “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this new event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

The name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

From crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

In an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a new, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

It follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he says, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

Unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he says. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”

Each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

Krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s says he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

The competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

Yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he says. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”

Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

Krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”

But the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he says. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”

Despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he says, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

#6637. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6635. Chanel’s Watches & Fine Jewelry Dinner Christened Daniel Humm’s New Hotspot

“Yes, it’s my first time here, too,” was the refrain repeatedly heard around the room at Humm on Hudson Street on Tuesday evening, as guests stole glances at their Première Galon watches to count down the minutes to dinner. After a candlelit cocktail hour, right on cue, at 8 p.m., the moment had come to experience Daniel Humm’s new restaurant, some two years in the making.

Chanel has been keeping New York’s best-dressed guests busy as of late: The last few weeks alone have seen outings for the Museum of Modern Art’s Film Benefit, the Dia Art Foundation, the Women’s Prize Trust, and Tribeca Through Her Lens. This time around, the annual Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner was as good an excuse as any for the group to get dolled up and enjoy a pause before the busiest season of all.

Sarah Pidgeon, who became an official ambassador for the house’s watches and fine jewelry last year, was among the earliest to arrive. For the occasion, the Love Story star donned a Coco Crush necklace and bracelets. The night was also a chance for the actress to reunite with fellow Ryan Murphy-universe newcomer Ella Beatty, fresh off her acclaimed turn as the notorious Lizzie Borden.

Though the restaurant has been open for just a month and change—Chanel’s get-together being the first brand event hosted there—word has traveled fast about its menu. Luckily, the evening’s sampling incorporated the soon-to-be-renowned caviar-topped miniature bagels, which, along with the disco-tiled bathroom, seem destined for Instagram Stories fame.

A crowd, including Ella Rubin, Jack Harlow, and Quen Blackwell, settled in, drinking up the oxblood and velvet interiors, co-designed by Pierre Yovanovitch and Humm’s longtime friend, Italian artist Francesco Clemente. Clemente—yes, the namesake of the bar at Humm’s Eleven Madison Park—covered the ceilings in hand-painted stars, bricks, tiles, and trains. Works by Louise Bourgeois, Rashid Johnson, and Roni Horn round out the feast for the eyes.

As chocolate mousses and endless trays of espresso martinis did the rounds and the clock struck 10 p.m., Pidgeon stood to introduce a surprise performance by breakthrough Canadian singer girlsweetvoiced to end the night. “I was listening to her earlier today while walking around New York, and she captures something that’s very tender and honest in her stories,” Pidgeon said. “Her music is both singular and expansive and entirely her own.”

After girlsweetvoiced serenaded the room with three songs—“Cranberry,” “Spearmint,” and “Tonight,” her Joni Mitchell–approved single that samples “California”—the night drew to a close. Guests slowly made their way toward the exit, taking engraved gold matchboxes home with them as a keepsake of a reliably good time with Chanel, no matter the theme.

So far, the noodles have only been spotted at select Costco warehouses. But if you don't want to wait for your local store to stock them, shoppers have also reported finding Jif ramen at retailers like Dollar Tree and Walmart.

#6633. Pride and Prejudice’s Rufus Sewell Is the Most Dashing Man on Television

It’s possible that Rufus Sewell is having too much fun right now. Between playing morally ambiguous Vice President (and husband to the U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James’s) Hal Wyler in Netflix’s frothy, prestige-y series The Diplomat and the beloved but deeply flawed Mr. Bennet in the streamer’s upcoming adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, he’s cornered the market on lovable rascals. He thrives on “exercises in gray” and relishes “when it goes wrong” for a character. “It’s the opposite of what you want in life,” he tells me. “You want drama, you want mistakes.” These roles offer plenty of both.

Wyler, of The Diplomat, is navigating how to work with the increasingly autocratic and bloody-minded President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) thousands of miles away from his wife Kate (Keri Russell), who is starting to exhibit some of his own manipulative behaviors she claims to abhor. Two centuries prior, Mr. Bennet is reckoning not with geopolitical crises and egomaniacal heads of state, but with the challenges his wife faces in marrying off five eligible, if dowry-poor, daughters.

Sewell sat down for a long chat with GQ about the two series, the value of blending high silliness with high stakes in the same scene, and how bodily functions are an under-appreciated key to unlocking a character’s specificity.

Rufus Sewell: The interesting question for me, for the second half of the season, was how much is Hal truly aware of everything that Kate and everyone else are noticing and concerned about with Grace's behavior. How much does he see? How much is he choosing to pretend not to see in order to stay in the room? He's always believed that access is all, but how much do you compromise in order to stay in the room? Where’s the point when you realize you stayed in the room too long without saying anything, and the moment’s passed, and you are just an accomplice? I found it very difficult to play his seeming unctuousness and obsequiousness with Grace this season, and to not be trying to protect my character in the wrong way, because I felt he was failing.

He’s overestimated his ability to effect change with Grace. Hal was prepared to appear to be supporting her, when he believed in his ability to steer her in a better direction, and I think he goes past that point. When I read the final episode script and saw where he ends up walking out, it gave me the courage to really lean into how much he goes wrong, by his own standards earlier in the season. He begins to lose his way in a way that he never has done before. But I embraced it, knowing that the real gift of the part was getting to play him going wrong and then seemingly correcting himself. We actually shot a speech that he made, just to give us a sense of where the scene was headed and for me to know how to play it. They might end up using some of it in the next season, or they could end up completely changing what was written. Hal coming out of the summit is a momentous decision in terms of what that does for the future and I've got no idea what’s next—I can't wait to start filming season five to find out.

I was always shocked when this show was described as a thriller because I always thought it was a kind of romantic sex comedy with extremely high stakes, because what it reminded me of firstly was some of the comedy of divorce screwball films of the 1940s. The characters may be divorced after a very tempestuous relationship, but they’re interlinked in a way that can never be undone. There's a romance to all of that history.

The other thing that it reminded me of was the kind of films that were made in the '70s—French films where halfway through an argument one of the characters would sit down on the toilet, you know what I mean? The people inside these films remind you of your own relationships. Your long-term relationship might not go to the same extremes, it might not be in the same setting, but I think people are people. What I love about their relationship is their shared wonkiness, and the getting into the nitty-gritty of the politics and taking someone down and hatching a plot whilst fighting over pastries and getting crumbs on the bed—all of that is part of their foreplay.

That is what the show is about, as far as I'm concerned. These are people who wear suits that might stand at a lectern and be on TV, but the fact is, how do you scratch an itch? Do you smell? Do you need to go to the toilet? These are the things that the script leans into a lot, and it might put some people off, but I don't care about that. That's the thing that makes it feel real, and it's so refreshing to play.

He'll flirt with anyone. We all know people like this. It's not even necessarily sexual, he just engages with people on that level and it's a natural thing for him.

I would say Hal’s flirtatiousness being a problem is open for debate, because a lot of what we understand of him is via Kate’s descriptions of him and his behavior. I can and often do see it in a different way. Part of the story of seasons three and four is Kate’s realization that a lot of stuff she thought of as his personality was in fact the mantle of the job that he'd taken on, because we see her doing the same kinds of things now that she is an ambassador. They both have a lot of the same qualities. They're both killers in a sense, and it's been very convenient for her and great for the show for her to introduce the public to Hal through her descriptions. And yet, every time it seems like he's changed character, in fact, it is revealing something from a different perspective.

We learned pretty early on that we were going to be doing some very, very long scenes, and we were given the advantage of seeing the scenes very early so we could slowly gestate the performances. We needed that because Windsor Castle in the show was comprised of several different buildings and locations, some of them with oceans between them, so we’d be shooting some parts the next day, and other bits in four months’ time.

Especially with a two-hander, with such long takes, you can go in and out of being relaxed, unrelaxed, free, slightly bound, and actually you get to the point where you stop worrying about it. It's like being on stage, because you end up too tired to be bad all the time and end up inhabiting the moment and things just happen. I love that all of it was a surprise to us.

I think what is most important in this particular iteration of the relationship between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet is that he comes to realize which ways he's failed his daughters. When Mrs. Bennet says to him in this version, it's easy for you to say that I’m silly or frivolous, but you try being a woman at this age with no means—this is the fight of their lives that he is making these jokes about. And yes, of course he's funny and right in certain ways, but he's also guilty of negligence of his family for the sake of an easy life for himself. The reason they have no money is that so much money has been spent on bonnets. Money could have been saved, but in order to have a quiet life, he's ducked out of fights in order to avoid responsibility.

Exactly. It was a gift in this role to have that moment when he feels that, admits that, and gets to be slightly humbled in this idea of himself that he's been cultivating. He didn’t actively or consciously avoid having this revelation, but that’s the effect of staying in his study, and now he’s facing the consequences. To use very modern terms, he has a revelation of what his pattern has been. It made sense!

One could be forgiven for thinking that Mr. and Mrs. Bennet are two people that used to be attracted to each other and now have nothing in common and don't like each other. I think it's born out in the book, though, the idea that there is still a love there, and especially a shared humor between them, and a bit of a spark remains.

I love the fact that we get to get drunk together and stuff like that. Olivia Colman and I worked on The Father together a few years ago with Anthony Hopkins, which was a very different kind of gig, but as is often the case with things that are very heavy and intense, we had a hoot doing it. I loved working with her, and was very excited about the chance to work with her again. I love the scenes between Mr. Bennet and Mrs. Bennet. They were such a treat for us.

#6632. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6630. Willy Chavarria Debuts His Dream “Bitchy Little Bags”

Are you a woman chasing the Willy Chavarria look? You’ll want to channel a Hitchcock heroine—Tippi Hedren is his favorite. Elongating skirt? Check. Strong-shouldered blouse or jacket? Done. Swooping french twist? Looking up Youtube tutorials now. But what about the classic handbag hitched up in the crook of your arm? Now, that can be yours, too.

Launched this morning on willychavarria.com, two new styles—the Bronca and the W Slouch—mark the New York designer’s official debut in the handbag space. Despite the pretty regular appearance of bags at his runway shows (both the Bronca and the W Slouch were seen at his spring 2027 menswear outing), introducing the category was a long time coming for Chavarria. “I’ve just been really timid about launching bags because it’s such a big thing,” he tells Vogue. “I never wanted to have a bag that ends up at the back of the store, doesn’t get the attention it needs—we just kind of pulled back and we said, okay, we’re going to launch this very soft bag that feels good.” Hence, only two styles, and direct-to-consumer only.

The Bronca is “sassy,” “a bitchy little bag,” even, and that’s just how Chavarria likes it. Available in pink, blue, black, and chocolate brown, it features a rolled leather handle with a set of keys dangling from the clasp. His dream girl to sport it is his forever muse Bianca Jagger; he’s fantasized about her pairing it with the iconic Yves Saint Laurent white wedding suit she wore to marry Mick in 1971.

In contrast, Chavarria says the W Slouch, available in green, chocolate brown, and black, is geared more towards his menswear customers. It comes with a detachable padded long strap, making it ideal for trekking across town with half of your belongings. To style it, he suggests following the wrong shoe theory. “I think it’s really cool with a tough look for a guy to have a bag that throws it off,” he says. “I always love those looks that just make you do a double take.”

Prior to today’s release, the designer has produced a W-embossed leather tote, some clutches, and a few coin purses, but he doesn’t look at those offerings in the same light. “This is more of me looking at [the category] as a business opportunity and building a plan and thinking about how I can grow this business,” he says.

It helps that with every collection, he’s dabbling in womenswear more and more. For his women customers, he sees a handbag as the perfect way in. “The brand is still small enough that I’m very careful about adding new categories, but as I’ve seen my womenswear business grow, it makes sense from a strategic standpoint to add a bag to the collection that actually enhances the full collection. And maybe she just buys the bag, maybe that’s all she wants.”

Though Chavarria is personally partial to a razor-sharp evening clutch, he doesn’t have plans to expand into additional silhouettes anytime soon. “I want to sit with these for a while,” he says. “I want to get these in the market and have people wearing them and get comfortable with them, and then maybe add on some little offspring, some little babies that go inside.” A nesting doll of handbag options await.

#6627. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6625. Harry Styles-Approved Designer Macy Grimshaw Just Won the 2026 H&M Design Award

Her off-kilter pieces have also been worn by Emma Corrin, Simone Ashley, and Anya Taylor-Joy.

Earlier this year, Macy Grimshaw presented her graduate collection from Central Saint Martins at London Fashion Week, styled by Harry Lambert, the mind behind the wardrobes of Emma Corrin, Alexander Skarsgård, and Harry Styles. Since then, the 25-year-old designer has continued to rise, dressing the likes of Anya Taylor-Joy, Simone Ashley, and several of Lambert’s clients—Corrin and Styles among them—in her semi-surrealist separates and top-notch leatherwork. Now, Grimshaw has a major accolade to cap off her standout year: the 2026 H&M Design Award.

At the presentation on Wednesday afternoon in London, Grimshaw was chosen among seven other finalists from top design universities across the globe: Chico Yu, Ennis Finnerty Mackay, Evelina Kryvopust, Fantin Delattre Pirenne, Jessica Lin, Macy Grimshaw, Yichun Liu, and Yvonne Schichtel. Grimshaw will receive a €150,000 ($164,655) endowment, a yearlong mentorship, and will have her collection produced and sold in selected H&M stores worldwide and online in October 2027. Each finalist was awarded a €10,000 ($10,980) endowment.

“She left me with desire and intrigue to see how she can actually develop the work,” said Beka Gvishiani, founder of Style Not Com, who joined H&M’s creative advisor Ann-Sofie Johansson, model Paloma Elsesser, and designer Ib Kamara on the jury. “For the moment, it’s very much the artist’s work,” he continued. “But she has ideas about how to make it wearable for daywear, because some of the pieces are great for an event or a performance.”

Gvishiani highlights the collection’s more experimental pieces, like a rusted, laser-cut mesh minidress ornamented with padlocks or a terracotta-hued molded bustier scattered with discarded cigarette butts. The scenography of the latter was inspired, naturally, by the brick wall where CSM students gather on smoke breaks.

But in between those more experimental moments, it’s easy to see why Grimshaw walked away with the prize, H&M’s first time awarding it since 2020. While fodder for celebrity placements and red carpets, her work also carries “hanger appeal,” clothes that are both wearable and appealing but also evoke something unexpected and slightly “off.” Like a texturized, scalloped suit jacket with a taut waist à la the “New Look” or the almost wet-looking crumpled silk slip dress done in a graphic, almost watercolor effect.

The line took cues from the designer’s college years in London (at 18, she moved there from Hong Kong to attend CSM) and speaks to her introspective way of working. “My whole practice is inspired by my grandmother having Alzheimer’s and trying to represent the fading of memories by using everyday objects and to recontextualize them,” Grimshaw told ELLE after the award was announced. “I want to remind us not to take the everyday for granted; that’s why a lot of my work is pencil shavings, cigarettes, locks.”

Next up, the designer will head to H&M’s home base of Stockholm, where she’ll get started on her collaboration with the brand. “This opportunity is going to be a massive help to make my work accessible to everyone,” she adds. “I’m very excited because this collection was not designed with the idea of commerciality. So I’m really interested to challenge myself and also work with other people to see how it can become that.”

#6624. How to Grow a Beard

So you want to learn how to grow a beard. First off, you should know that it helps to have the right genetics. Second, you have to stay committed to the endeavor. Too often, beard-growing attempts end before they’ve even had a chance to establish itself.

“I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, says. “Your beard needs time to actually show you what it’s going to look like, and that growth period lets you see the natural direction everything’s growing in. Plus, some hairs take longer to come in than others, so patience is key.”

There’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack. These are the best tips to maximize your hair follicles’ potential whether this is your first beard or your fiftieth.

There are many different beard styles to choose from; you don’t need to stick to neatly manicured, uniform look. Let your growth be influenced by the style you want to achieve.

“Your genes determine hair thickness, growth rate, density, and color,” Mendoza says. “If your dad or granddad had a thin beard, you’re probably dealing with the same hand, and that’s just life.”

If your beard is patchy, or if it has a unique growth pattern (sparse on the cheeks, full on the goatee, for example), then you should set your expectations properly. This goes for beards big, small, and medium alike. And while nutrition is important for hair growth, you can’t cheat genetics with your diet.

Patience is a virtue. Not only can a little time help fill in some patchiness, but it’s also requisite for almost any style. A beard transforms into something new every week. So, if it’s seeming like you’ll never reach your goal—in particular if it’s a long beard—then you honestly might wake up one morning and realize that you’ve arrived at the destination.

Mendoza says to wait at least two weeks before you start to do a cleanup, but only around the ends, i.e. the hairs that aren’t within the perimeter in which you want your beard to grow. That’ll help you figure out your beard’s natural shape.

One of the tenets of beard maintenance is to keep it defined. In short: shave the neckline and clean up the cheek lines. These keep it more beard-like and less neckbeard-like—unless, for some reason, a wooly stoner beard is your aim. In that case, let it grow wild and free.

The second way to keep things looking intentional is to sculpt and trim your beard as it grows. It might feel counterproductive—and counter to #2—but it’s the same way you need to get haircuts while growing out your hair. As Mendoza says, this helps direct the hair exactly where it needs to be: Fuller in some spots, less so in others. The styling products in the next tip can of course help influence things, but you foremost want to keep hairs in check as needed: This can mean spot-checking strays, snipping away split ends, or simply taking out some bulk. You’ll want a beard trimmer or a sharp pair of scissors.

There are a handful of beard products you should consider picking up if you’re serious about proper care and maintenance. A few drops of beard oil will absorb quickly and give your hair the right nutrients (plus a pinch of shine), while also making it less wild and frizzy. You can also swap in a beard balm or cream, something slightly heftier than an oil, to help style the beard and keep it in place all day. What’s important is that you clean your beard every day with an actual beard wash and not just a regular shampoo, which Mendoza says will dry out your beard and your face.

Weekly maintenance will consist of a deep condition, which you can do in the shower. “If you’re doing those things consistently, your beard is going to look way healthier and fuller than most guys out there,” he says.

Beard brushes help exfoliate the skin beneath the beard, for starters, which lifts dead skin cells and prevents future flaking. Moreover, brushing your beard at the end of each day will ensure its health and tame-ability in the long haul. This distributes the natural oils produced in the skin, which otherwise collect at the base of the shaft and only nourish the bottom of each hair. This oil distribution prevents breakage, frizzing, and split ends. (This is a great time to apply a few drops of beard oil as a booster, especially after a shower.)

Once your base has grown out—this can take months—it’s time to really make it yours. One of our favorites is to snip the bridge between the mustache and the chin, thus marooning the mustache. Or, pare back the beard itself, leaving a fuller mustache. You have lots of options, and it’s your privilege as a beard grower to flaunt it.

#6623. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

Even if PB&J isn't your jam (get it?), General Mills has other additions on the way, including Ghost Protein Cereal x Trix and Annie's Protein Cereal in Honey and Berry Vanilla flavors. Just judging by that lineup alone, 2027 is shaping up to be a pretty protein-packed year in the cereal aisle.

#6621. The Vogue Business People Moves Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business People Moves Tracker, a running list highlighting the key executive appointments and exits across the fashion and beauty industries. From CEOs to creative directors to other key C-suite hires, we track the leadership shifts that are reshaping the industry.

Background: Alessandro Pungetti has been appointed head designer and creative director of Japanese brand White Mountaineering, starting with the FW27 season. Pungetti previously held roles as knitwear designer at Stone Island before joining CP Company as head designer across all collections. In 2009, he founded Ten C with Paul Harvey, who he previously collaborated with at Stone Island.

Company comments: “While inheriting the core values ​​of White Mountaineering, [Alessandro] will also pioneer new possibilities, leading to the brand’s further development,” the press release said.

Background: Justin Boxford has been appointed CEO of Capri Holdings, following John D Idol’s announcement that he will retire as chairman and CEO after two decades of leadership. Boxford joins from The Estée Lauder Companies, where he most recently served as global president, luxury beauty brands. He previously served as global brand president of Estée Lauder. To support the transition, Idol will serve as a senior advisor to Capri Holdings through March 31.

Company comments: “We are confident that Justin is the right leader to guide Capri in its next chapter of growth,” said Robin Freestone, incoming independent chairman of the board. “He brings an exceptional track record of revitalizing and growing global luxury and beauty brands, deep international experience and a people-centered leadership approach.”

“It has been an extraordinary privilege to lead Capri for the past 23 years,” said Idol. “I am immensely proud of what we have accomplished together. I have had the opportunity to work with Justin in the past while he helped build the Michael Kors fragrance business at The Estée Lauder Companies and have watched his successes over the years. I am confident he is the ideal person to lead Capri into the future.”

Background: Jonatan Janmark has stepped down as CEO of Circulose (formerly Renewcell), with CFO Amanda Geijer appointed to lead the business in the interim. In 2024, textile-to-textile recycler Renewcell filed for bankruptcy, having struggled to get the brand buy-in needed to keep its commercial-scale production facility in Sweden afloat. Former McKinsey partner Janmark was appointed CEO the same year, after renaming the company to Circulose under the ownership of private equity firm Altor. Now, Janmark has stepped down, having completed his mandate of securing enough brand partnerships to restart the production plant. Geijer will take over with the support of executive chair Helena Helmersson.

Company comments: “When Jonatan joined, Circulose had just been given a second chance. Since then, he has made Circulose a leading player in textile-to-textile recycling again. That has taken a lot of energy, creativity and teamwork. I have learnt a lot from working with Jonatan, and I want to thank him for everything he has built,” Helmersson said in a statement. “For the upcoming phase, I am very pleased that Amanda, who knows the company and our plans well, has agreed to lead Circulose as interim CEO until a permanent CEO is in place.”

Background: Caroline Deroche Pasquier joins Dior in a newly created role as director of press, VIP and cultural relations. She began her career at Saint Laurent before joining LVMH, where she worked at Louis Vuitton and Givenchy. During the last six years, Pasquier has led global communications for Bottega Veneta and then Versace. At Dior, she will work closely with the house’s creative director Jonathan Anderson, reporting to Olivier Bialobos, deputy managing director in charge of global communication and image.

Company comments: “[Deroche Pasquier’s] career spans communication, creative collaboration, international markets and cultural relationships, giving her a broad perspective on the development and expression of luxury brands,” the company said in a statement.

Background: Oliver Timm has voluntarily stepped down from Hugo Boss, where he’s been both chief sales officer and deputy CEO since 2024, as well as the company board. In the meantime, CEO Daniel Grieder, alongside CFO and COO Ivica Maric, will split Timm’s previous duties. Timm was initially appointed as chief sales officer in 2021, to oversee Hugo Boss’s two brands (Boss and Hugo), including wholesale, e-commerce, visual merchandizing, retail operations, and customer relations.

The announcement follows Hugo Boss’s 5% sales drop in Q3 — attributed to an ongoing turnaround at the company — and Frasers Group’s de-facto takeover of the company on October 23.

Company comments: “Oliver Timm and I have been working side by side throughout our careers for almost 30 years, and it is a great honor for me to look back on this time and the many moments we have shared. I will miss working alongside him,” said Grieder in a statement. “During his time at Hugo Boss, he has repositioned sales with a future-oriented omnichannel approach and a strong customer-centric mindset, making a significant contribution to our growth and digitalization. As I look back at these achievements, I wish him, also on behalf of the entire managing board, the very best for the future.”

Michael Murray, Hugo Boss chair and Frasers Group CEO, also shared his appreciation: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Oliver Timm for his contribution to Hugo Boss over the past years. We appreciate his commitment and wish him all the best for his professional and personal future.”

Background: Ben Hallam, most recently SVP of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, has been appointed as Lululemon’s chief brand officer. At the sportswear brand, Hallam will lead global brand marketing, brand creative, store experience, and community. He will join the company’s senior leadership team and report to CEO Heidi O’Neill who joined in April 2026.

The announcement comes after the appointments of Maggie Gauger as president and chief product officer and Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. On Friday, the company also announced the appointment of Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective November 23. Sunderland joins from Boston Consulting Group and will report to chief financial officer Meghan Frank. Searches remain underway for a chief technology officer and a chief communications officer.

Company comments: “Ben brings an exceptional combination of creative vision, commercial discipline, and experience transforming iconic, premium brands at scale,” O’Neill said in a statement. “His proven ability to translate brand strategy into distinctive and compelling guest experiences will be critical as we strengthen how our brand comes to life across every touchpoint. Ben will play a central role in building a stronger and more competitive Lululemon.”

Background: Daisy Shaw-Ellis has been appointed CMO of Malone Souliers, where she will oversee the brand’s global marketing and communications, with an emphasis on expansion in North America. Shaw-Ellis joins from Condé Nast, where she was most recently accessories and jewelry director for Vogue and Vanity Fair.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Daisy to Malone Souliers as global chief marketing officer,” CEO Andrew Wright said in a statement. “Her experience in executive positions at some of the industry’s most established and influential titles, alongside her exceptional eye and proven track record in luxury brand-building, will both enhance and amplify our voice globally. This is a pivotal moment for Malone Souliers as we embark on a new and exciting trajectory, and we look forward to presenting the brand in new and exciting ways in the coming seasons.”

Background: Clarisse Godbillon, who was CFO and COO of Lemaire from 2020 to 2025, is returning to the brand as managing director. She left Lemaire in 2025 to become COO of Jacquemus, and made the move back to the French label after Laetitia Mergui stepped down from the head job earlier this year.

Company comments: “Clarisse possesses an in-depth understanding of the company’s various activities and a profound knowledge of its identity,” the house said in a statement. “As managing director, she will oversee the development of the brand and lead its strategic and operational direction, working closely with [the house’s artistic directors and majority shareholders] Christophe Lemaire and Sarah-linh Tran.”

Background: Lady Gaga has moved into the CEO role at Haus Labs, the clean beauty company she founded in 2019. This comes after co-founder and former CEO Ben Jones exited the brand in early October. Gaga will now lead all commercial aspects of Haus Labs, alongside her prior responsibilities of creative direction and product development.

Background: Ryan Lally has been promoted to chief brand communications officer at Ralph Lauren Corp. Formerly SVP of global public relations and brand communications, Lally will continue to build on the company’s global comms strategy in this newly created role, while overseeing talent partnerships, events and more. Lally has been with the company for more than two decades, and will continue to report to David Lauren, chief branding and innovation officer.

Background: Alexis Hoopes, formerly global fashion VP at Ebay, has joined The RealReal as chief merchandising officer. At Ebay, she led the company’s $10 billion global fashion business for two-plus years, including the expansion of its Authenticity Guarantee program to new categories, price points and markets, strengthening trust among buyers and sellers. Hoopes will now lead The RealReal’s merchandising strategy, focusing on its luxury assortment and personalized product discovery — as the platform further advances its AI capabilities and unlocks growth opportunities.

Company comments: “Alexis is a proven leader who brings a rare combination of luxury merchandising expertise, global marketplace experience and operational discipline,” Rati Sahi Levesque, president and CEO of The RealReal, said in a statement. “As we build on our leadership in luxury resale, her ability to connect exceptional merchandise with evolving consumer demand will be instrumental in accelerating growth.”

Background: Hector Muelas joined LVMH in 2015 as global VP of content and creative, after working for Apple. Between 2017 and 2019, he was chief brand officer of LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa under chief executive Alexandre Arnault. Muelas then returned to Apple as global group creative director in 2019, a role he held until 2021. He returned to LVMH in 2023 as Tiffany & Co.’s global chief brand and creative officer, reuniting with Alexandre Arnault.

He has now been named Louis Vuitton chief brand creative officer, a newly created position reporting to Louis Vuitton deputy CEO Damien Bertrand.

Company comments: “Hector will define and steer our creative storytelling across all touchpoints, thereby ensuring strong overall image consistency. Leading creative and content execution, he will oversee all brand campaigns, with the art buying team led by Magena Chansarel and the content factory team led by Carole Fuchs joining his organization. In close collaboration with our business units, regions, and creative talents, Hector will further elevate our brand desirability, ensuring the house continues to set the benchmark in cultural resonance, creative boldness, and emotional connection with our clients worldwide,” Bertrand said in an internal announcement.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky, who most recently exited the board at Chanel, but remains president of Chanel SAS and fashion, is now co-chair of The Fashion Pact. A non-profit organization, The Fashion Pact is a coalition of CEOs from more than 150 companies representing a third of the global fashion industry by volume. Pavlovsky will work alongside Inditex CEO Óscar García Maceiras and climate campaigner Paul Polman to build on the work of the pact in creating a net-zero fashion industry. (Chanel is among the coalition’s founding signatories back in 2019.)

Company comments: “As we look ahead to 2027, our focus is increasingly on translating collective ambition into implementation, and scaling solutions across the industry. Bruno’s appointment marks an important step in this journey, bringing valuable leadership and perspective as we work to strengthen collaboration across regions, business models and supply chains,” The Fashion Pact wrote on LinkedIn.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky joined Chanel in 1990 and became a board member in 2018, a duty he will now step down from. Since 2022, he has also been president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Pavlovsky remains president of Chanel SAS and of the house’s fashion activities.

Company comments: “This latest move marks the completion of the board’s evolution toward a composition of independent directors, bringing diverse external expertise and perspectives, while retaining executive representation through the global executive chair and global CEO. Bruno Pavlovsky remains fully committed to his role as president of Chanel’s fashion activities and president of Chanel SAS,” Chanel said in a statement.

Background: Zankov has appointed Jack Tobin, founder of luxury brand development consultancy Jack Tobin Agency, as CEO and business partner of Zankov, formalizing a partnership that has developed since Tobin began consulting for the brand two years ago. Since beginning its partnership with Jack Tobin Agency, Zankov has increased its international business more than tenfold and doubled its global stockist network.

Company comments: “Zankov is at an incredibly exciting stage in its growth. I have always envisioned having a partner who could join me in shaping the next chapter of the brand — someone who shares my ambition to build an enduring business while staying true to the creative vision that has always defined Zankov. Jack is the ideal partner to take this next step with, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” says Henry Zankov, founder and creative director.

Background: Net-a-Porter (NAP) has appointed Devina Foley as Americas president to oversee the retailer’s US and Canada strategy. With more than 20 years of experience across retail, merchandising and e-commerce, Foley will help strengthen NAP’s market positioning as it settles into a new era under LuxExperience Group. She has held senior leadership roles at Bandier, Rockets of Awesome and Gilt, following earlier positions at Loft and Gap Inc. Based in New York, Foley will report to NAP CEO Heather Kaminetsky.

Company comments: “Devina brings an impressive breadth of experience and a proven track record of driving growth and leading businesses through transformation,” Kaminetsky said in a statement. “Her leadership and expertise will be invaluable as we continue to grow Net-a-Porter’s US business.”

Background: LVMH has promoted Clara Boissonnas, formerly women’s leather goods product director at Louis Vuitton, to CEO of Pucci. Boissonnas joined Louis Vuitton in 2002 as a product manager, before exiting four years later. After a decade working across Lanvin and Byredo, she returned to LV where she helped shape the maison’s coveted leather goods business. At Pucci, Boissonnas will strengthen the brand’s distinctive creative identity, desirability, and international reach, while reporting to Pietro Beccari, chair and CEO of the LVMH Fashion Group. As for Saar Debrouwere, who has led Pucci since 2022, her future role will be announced in due course, according to the group.

Company comments: “Clara has made a significant contribution to Louis Vuitton through her deep product expertise, strong creative sensibility, and unwavering commitment to excellence. Her ability to combine creative ambition with a clear understanding of the business makes her ideally suited to lead Pucci into its next chapter,” Beccari said in a statement.

Background: Yanina Novitskaya, who has spent the last 19 years at Cartier, most recently as CEO of South East Asia and Oceania, is the next chief executive of Richemont-owned Delvaux. Delvaux, the world’s oldest fine leather goods house, was founded in Brussels in 1829. In its next chapter, Novitskaya succeeds Jean-Marc Loubier, who returned to lead the brand after its acquisition in 2021, and will report to Richemont fashion and accessories CEO Philippe Fortunado.

Company comments: “Yanina’s strong knowledge of the luxury industry will be instrumental in leading Delvaux into its next chapter, strengthening its distinctive positioning and continuing to drive product desirability and international growth,” Fortunato said in a statement.

Background: Marc Jacobs has appointed John Wattiker as CMO to lead the brand’s global marketing strategy. Wattiker joins the brand after almost 15 years at Hearst Magazines working in the company’s advertising business, where he most recently held the role of VP of fashion and luxury. Prior to Hearst, he worked in the banking sector. At Marc Jacobs, Wattiker will oversee efforts to strengthen brand positioning, deepen consumer engagement and further expand the recently acquired brand’s global reach and relevance under new owner WHP Global.

Company comments: “John brings deep experience across luxury, fashion and media, with a clear understanding of how to build brands and engage consumers,” Marc Jacobs CEO Eric Marechalle said in a statement. “He pairs creative instinct with strategic and commercial discipline and brings an extensive network of relationships built over the course of his career. I am confident he will be a great addition to our leadership team as we grow Marc Jacobs globally.”

Background: Chanel has appointed a creative makeup director, Lucia Pieroni. Previously, Pieroni was creative director of makeup at Shiseido-owned Clé de Peau Beauté (2006-2019), which led to a series of partnerships with photographers and designers where Pieroni helped shape beauty direction for fashion shows, editorials, and campaigns. At Chanel, she will work alongside the makeup creation studio reporting to Simona Cattaneo, president of fragrance and beauty.

Company comments: “Lucia possesses an extraordinary instinct for beauty. She perceives the individuality in every face and understands with precision how to reveal it, creating makeup that feels intuitive and expressive, while always celebrating singularity. Her artistic vision and unique savoir-faire will make this collaboration a decisive new chapter for Chanel Makeup,” Cattaneo said in a statement.

Background: Alistair McCallum, formerly global communications VP at Burberry, has been appointed chief marketing officer of Givenchy. McCallum arrives with international comms experience at fellow LVMH house Fendi, and before that, at Alexander McQueen, where he worked with now-Givenchy creative director Sarah Burton. He will report to brand CEO Amandine Ohayon.

Company comments: “The arrival of Alistair McCallum [...] on our executive committee brings recognized expertise in the luxury and fashion worlds to support our international ambition and teams worldwide,” Ohayon said in a statement.

Background: LVMH-owned jewelry brand Repossi has appointed Matthieu Soudan as managing director. The hire comes as the brand’s former CEO Anne de Vergeron returns to her management responsibilities at the LVMH group level. Soudan has been in the LVMH ecosystem for nine years, the majority of which were spent as general manager of Tag Heuer before moving to Bvlgari in 2025. At Repossi, he will lead the brand into its next phase within the world of contemporary high jewelry, while strengthening its positioning and global reach.

Company comments: “I am delighted to entrust the leadership of Repossi to Matthieu Soudan as we open a new chapter in the development of this distinctive maison. At Tag Heuer and more recently at Bvlgari, he has demonstrated a strong strategic vision, together with the ability to execute strategies that support operational excellence and the desirability of our maisons,” Stéphane Bianchi, group managing director and CEO of LVMH Watches & Jewelry, said in a statement.

Background: Capri has appointed Catherine So as the company’s chief legal and sustainability officer. So joins from Tiffany & Co., where she most recently served as senior vice president and general counsel, where she oversaw legal, compliance, intellectual property, litigation, governance and brand protection. She spent 15 years at Tiffany across various roles.

Company comments: “We are pleased to welcome Catherine to Capri Holdings. She is a highly respected legal leader with extensive experience with helping develop global luxury brands and executive teams through periods of transformation and growth,” CEO John D. Idol said in a statement. “Her expertise, leadership, and strategic perspective will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen our business and position our brands for long-term success.”

Background: Poshmark has made a string of executive hires. Creative consultant Jamie Hunter, who worked as a buyer and fashion director at Bergdorf Goodman, has been appointed fashion and creative director of the California-based resale company. This new role signals Poshmark’s ambition to become an authority in the fashion resale space, by bringing its curation, styling and creative direction in-house, informed by Hunter’s two-plus decades in the industry.

Other new hires include: Yoshitaka Matsuzawa as SVP of seller and community experience, leading product development across consumer experiences and AI; Kishore Kumar Mohan (formerly The RealReal) as engineering SVP; Lesley Clifford as VP of merchandising, also a new role supporting a more strategic approach to assortment and brand relationships; and Beth Newman (formerly Canada Goose) as PR and communications director.

Company comments: “We’ve been deliberate about bringing in leaders who add deep expertise in their respective fields and fresh perspectives to Poshmark. With experience spanning fashion, technology and retail, they’re strengthening our leadership team and helping us sharpen our fashion point of view,” chief revenue officer Elizabeth von der Goltz said in a statement.

Background: Stephan Sturm has decided to step down as chair and member of the supervisory board of Hugo Boss, following discussions between the brand and its now-largest shareholder Frasers Group. The Mike Ashley-owned business upped its stake in the German brand in mid-August, from 30.28%% to 47.89%; the rising share comes on the heels of Frasers’s June takeover bid of £1.72 billion, which the Hugo Boss board deemed “inadequate” and urged shareholders to reject.

Now the largest shareholder of the Hugo Boss business, Frasers Group is edging closer to expanding to its portfolio further, following the acquisition of UK department store Harvey Nichols last month. Sturm will continue to serve as chair until a successor has been elected.

Company comments: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Stephan Sturm for his leadership, commitment, and dedication to Hugo Boss. We respect his decision and will work closely with him to ensure a smooth transition,” deputy chair Sinan Piskin said in a statement.

Background: Space NK has named Emma Simpson-Scott as CEO, succeeding Andy Lightfoot, who is stepping down after a decade heading the beauty retailer. Following a period of significant growth and transformation, including its recent acquisition by Ulta Beauty, Simpson-Scott will now lead the business as it matures further. Previously, the executive spent seven and a half years as CMO and 10 years at Space NK altogether.

Company comments: “Under Andy’s leadership, Space NK achieved significant growth, strengthened its position as a market-leading beauty retailer, and successfully transitioned into the Ulta Beauty family,” Kecia Steelman, president CEO of parent company Ulta Beauty, said in a statement. “Emma is a highly respected retail leader who brings deep customer insight, retail expertise and a passion for building exceptional teams. I look forward to our continued work together as she leads Space NK into the next chapter of growth.”

Background: Southern Californian brand St. John has named former co-creative director of Kenzo Humberto Leon as creative director. Beyond Kenzo, Leon co-founded fashion concept store Opening Ceremony in 2002 and is best known for his distinctive multidisciplinary approach to design. At St. John, Leon will oversee the knitwear brand’s image, design, and overall creative direction.

Company comments: “Humberto brings a rare instinct for honoring our history while making it feel entirely new. He understands that true luxury lives in how clothing makes people feel, which is the very spirit Marie Gray built this house on. Together, we’re introducing St. John to a new generation who may not have felt it was made for them until now,” CEO Mandy West said in a statement.

Background: Richemont has appointed Anton Rupert as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board. Rupert, the son of Richemont chair Johann Rupert, has served as a non-executive director on Richemont’s board since 2017. He served as director of Watchfinder from July 2018 until December 2019. Since January 2021, he has served on the advisory board of Asia Partners Fund LP I, a regional Southeast Asia private equity fund focused on growth-stage technology-based opportunities. Following the meeting of Richemont’s board of directors on September 8, Richemont announced his appointment as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board of directors. He will serve alongside Bram Schot, who was appointed non-executive deputy chair in 2024 and who will continue in his role.

Company comments: “This appointment is an important step in the board’s long-term succession planning,” Richemont chairman Johann Rupert said in a statement. “Richemont’s strength has always rested on the continuity that comes from close family involvement, on rigorous governance, and on an unwavering commitment to creativity and craftsmanship. Having Anton and Bram serve together as non-executive co-deputy chairmen ensures that each of these foundations is given the attention it deserves: Anton will continue to safeguard the creative and product priorities that define our maisons, while Bram will ensure that our governance remains of the highest standard.”

Background: James Kelly has been named CEO of Theory, after joining the brand in 2022 as CFO and later as global co-chief operating officer. As global CEO of both Theory and Helmut Lang, Kelly will oversee both brands’ headquarters functions, commercial operations, and global growth initiatives. Before joining Theory, Kelly helped scale Uniqlo’s US expansion. He succeeds Dinesh Tandon, who will transition into the co-chief operating officer role, as well as returning to his role as CEO of Theory China.

Company comments: “James has been an instrumental leader for Theory over the past several years, bringing strategic vision, operational excellence and a deep understanding of our business,” said Kazumi Yanai, chairman of Theory. “As James assumes the role of global CEO and Dinesh focuses his leadership on one of our most important markets, we are further expanding our global organization and positioning Theory for continued success around the world.”

Background: Charlotte Fournet, the niece of Kering chair François-Henri Pinault, has been named CEO of jewelry maison Pomellato, succeeding Kering Italia president Sabina Belli. Fournet joined Saint Laurent in 2014 before moving to Gucci in 2019 and then Bottega Veneta in 2020, where she climbed the merchandising ladder to become director just over three years ago. Krizia Cucurachi, who joined Dodo in 2024 as global product and brand director, has been promoted to CEO. Prior to joining the brand, she spent more than a decade at Swarovski across several senior leadership positions. Both will report to Kering Jewelry CEO Jean-Marc Duplaix, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Jewelry is a strategic growth pillar for Kering. Pomellato and Dodo are two highly distinctive houses with strong identities and tremendous potential. Charlotte’s extensive experience across several Kering houses and Krizia’s strong track record in brand-building and transformation make them ideally positioned to lead the next phase of growth for Pomellato and Dodo,” Duplaix said in a statement.

Background: Sabina Belli, who joined Kering as CEO of Pomellato in 2015, has been named president of Kering Italia. Before joining the French luxury group, Belli held senior marketing and executive roles at WPP, L’Oréal Luxe and LVMH, spanning the likes of Christian Dior Parfums, Moët Hennessy, Veuve Clicquot, and Bvlgari. Since this April, she has also led Kering Accademia per le Eccellenze, a Kering initiative dedicated to preserving and promoting Italian craftsmanship, alongside serving on the directors board of the Kering Foundation. In her new role, Belli will report directly to CEO Luca de Meo, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Italy occupies a unique place in Kering’s history, identity, and future. Its creativity, craftsmanship, and industrial excellence are at the heart of our houses and the long-term vitality of the luxury industry,” de Meo said in a statement. “Sabina brings a deep understanding of the Italian luxury ecosystem and a strong ability to build partnerships across business, education and public institutions.”

Background: Kristin Bauer, who spent three years as chief supply chain officer for sneaker retailer Foot Locker, will join Converse as chief operating officer. As parent company Nike works to revive its Converse business, following consecutive quarters of slow sales, it is rebuilding a leadership structure to help propel growth. Bauer will report to Nike COO Venky Alagirisamy.

Company comments: “We are excited to welcome Kristin and look forward to the perspective she will bring as we continue to build momentum for the brand,” Nike said in a statement.

Background: Jane Ewing has been named chief commercial officer and executive vice president of Nike, reporting directly to CEO Elliott Hill. She joins after a 14-year tenure at Walmart, most recently serving as interim CEO for Sam’s Club China. She also previously held senior leadership roles at Diageo. In her new role, Ewing will lead Nike’s global marketplace organization, including Sales and Nike Direct.

Company’s comments: “Jane’s experience, leadership and global perspective will help us continue this work and accelerate growth across Nike Direct and wholesale. Her role is vital to creating even stronger connections between brand, product and marketplace while serving athletes* and consumers around the world,” Hill said in a statement.

Background: The British Fashion Council (BFC) has announced that David Pemsel is stepping down as chair after four years in the position and 10 years on the executive board. During his time as chair, the BFC achieved record revenue figures (£14 million in FY2024/25), raised £7.2 million through the BFC Foundation and secured a multi-million-pound investment from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. Pemsel also appointed Laura Weir as BFC CEO in early 2025. A successor will be announced in September.

Company comments: “David has been an exceptional chair and an unwavering champion of British fashion. His leadership has helped strengthen the British Fashion Council as an organization, creating the stability, governance and long-term foundations that enable us to deliver our ambitions for the industry,” Weir said in a statement.

Background: Alexandre Oulès has been named chief operating officer for the LVMH beauty division, reporting to Véronique Courtois, president and CEO of Parfums Christian Dior and of the LVMH Group’s beauty division. According to the internal announcement, his new role will “oversee manufacturing, supply chain, and purchasing across the beauty division, driving stronger convergence between maisons across all three functions”. Oulès joins from Balenciaga, where he was appointed COO in October 2023. He previously held roles at L’Oréal, Guerlain, Celine and Moët Hennessy.

Company’s comment: “I am delighted to welcome back Alexandre, whose pursuit of operational excellence is widely recognized. His knowledge of the group and the specificities of the beauty world will strongly contribute to the overall efficiency of our operations,” Courtois said.

Background: Maya Dukes, who previously worked at Macy’s as head of graphic design (2001-2007), will return to the retailer as executive creative director. Dukes has more than two decades of experience leading creative strategy for some of the world’s best-known consumer brands, including her most recent role leasing global creative at Delta Airlines. At Macy’s, Dukes will report to CMO Sharon Otterman, overseeing the company’s creative and storytelling to bring the Macy’s brand back to life and help propel its Bold New Chapter strategy.

Company comments: “I am excited to welcome Maya back to Macy’s. Her experience translating brand strategy into compelling storytelling, elevating the customer experience and modernizing the creative process will be critical as we strengthen Macy’s for the future,” Otterman said in a statement.

Background: Skims has appointed its first-ever chief design officer, Erin Magee, best known for her time at Supreme, where she spent over 20 years. Most recently she held the role of chief creative officer, under which she led the brand’s creative vision, design, product development, and product strategy across apparel, accessories, collaborations, and special projects. Skims has also promoted Kim Schraub, who has been on board since Skims’s founding, to chief brand officer from her previous role as creative director. In her new role, Schraub will balance creative and commercial. Prior to joining Skims, Schraub worked at Abercrombie, Victoria’s Secret Pink and Yeezy.

Company comments: “Erin brings an unparalleled creative vision and a proven ability to build brands that transcend fashion and become cultural touchstones,” CEO and co-founder Jens Grede said in a statement. “Her eye for design, her deep understanding of product and her instinct for what resonates make her exactly the right person to lead Skims into its next era. We’re incredibly excited to welcome her to the team.”

“Kim has been with us since before Skims existed. She helped turn an idea into a brand that people genuinely love,” Kim Kardashian, Skims chief creative officer and co-founder, said in a statement. “Her creative instincts have helped shape everything about how Skims shows up in the world, and this promotion is a reflection of the enormous impact she has had, and the trust Jens and I have in her vision. I can’t wait to see where she takes us next.”

Background: Vuori has appointed Carey Collins Krug as CMO. She joins from Abercrombie & Fitch, where she spent the last seven years, four of which she held the CMO role. Prior to Abercrombie, Collins Krug held top marketing positions at David Yurman, Ralph Lauren and Donna Karan. At Vuori, she will lead the brand’s cross-channel marketing initiatives, and focus on global expansion.

Company comments: “Carey brings the kind of brand-building, consumer engagement and cross-functional marketing leadership that will be instrumental as Vuori enters its next chapter of growth,” Joe Kudla, founder and CEO of Vuori, said in a statement. “Her experience helping global lifestyle brands sharpen their storytelling and build deeper connections with consumers aligns closely with where we’re headed as we continue to scale.”

Background: Rains has appointed Tom Bettinson as CEO, succeeding co-founder Daniel Brix Hesselager, who will transition into a business development role after leading the company for a year and a half. Since the initiatives core to Brix Hesselager’s transformation plan, in particular retail development, have been implemented, the focus will now shift to driving commercial success through these investments. Bettinson first joined Rains in 2017, helping to establish the brand’s UK business, before stepping away and rejoining as CSO, with responsibility for all company sales channels, in 2025.

Company comments: “I stepped into the CEO role to lead a fundamental transformation of our concept and organization. It was an extensive undertaking that required swift decision-making. Today, the foundation is in place, and the time is right to pass the baton,” Brix Hesselager said in a statement. “The priority now is ensuring excellence in execution and driving commercial success across all areas of the business. Tom is the right person to lead that next phase.”

Background: Pandora has appointed André Branch as president of North America, one of the Danish jewelry brand’s largest growth markets. Branch brings more than 25 years of experience across global consumer, beauty and lifestyle brands, most recently having served as CEO at Ariana Grande’s R.e.m. Beauty. At Pandora, he will lead the business’s next phase of regional growth, focusing specifically on enhancing customer relevance and brand appeal. Branch is succeeding Luciano Rodembusch, who departed the company in February.

Company comments: “André is a highly accomplished commercial leader with a strong track record of driving growth across global consumer businesses. His ability to combine strategic clarity with disciplined execution makes him exactly the right person to lead our North America business and drive the next phase of growth in the region,” chief commercial officer Massimo Basei said in a statement.

Background: Skims has hired Jasmine Sevan as vice president of communications. With nearly two decades of experience, Sevan will play a key role in advancing Skims’s global communication efforts, further strengthening its position at the intersection of fashion, culture, and innovation. She most recently served as global communications and brand partnerships director at Victoria Beckham, where she led the comms strategy during a period of significant growth, spurred by the brand’s Paris Fashion Week debut, collaborations with Mango and Gap, and the global launch of Netflix documentary, Victoria Beckham. At Skims, Sevan will report to chief communications officer Tracy Nguyen.
